negative.author: @logicalparadox2897
negative.text:
I think the biggest problem is that modern medicine isn’t trying to treat people, INDIVIDUAL PEOPLE. Rather, they are trying to treat the population as a whole. They view you and I as essentially the same people, with the same targets. They measure things, sometimes lots of things, but my doctor only looks to see if a given value is green or red (ie, they look for things “out of range”). They seem to fully trust the lab ranges, without realizing that many of these ranges are simply based on what is “normal” (typical) for the general population. Because they are looking for acute problems, not trying to troubleshoot chronic mysterious symptoms you may be dealing with, and definitely not to optimize health and wellbeing and give advice on how well your current diet and lifestyle are doing. You’re just one of many patients, a dot on a bell curve.

This is not medicine; it’s PUBLIC HEALTH. And it’s based on the potentially false assumption that all of us are basically the same or that any differences average out. They don’t seem to allow for the possibility that what might be a very healthy diet for one person might be disastrous for someone else. They don’t seem to appreciate how interconnected things like diet and lifestyle are and how many complex dependencies and relationships there are. The advice we give is just … bad. Because it’s all generality. 

We should be screening people for signs of atherosclerosis, and once signs show up, troubleshooting what is going on with THAT person, rather than just a generic protocol they prescribe for all patients. We should be looking at not just bio markers, but genetics, Epigenetics, and looking for better diagnostics that can help ascertain what is actually going on in the body. Instead of telling someone to eat a low salt diet for hypertension, how about actually finding what is causing the hypertension in that person, and then basing treatment on targeting those systems. 

We already know that nutritionism is broken at the philosophical level. For some people, they can’t convert certain forms of nutrients to active forms efficiently (folic acid methylation, for example, or converting beta carotene to vitamin A)… yet our nutritional advice does not account for these types of things. If you’re low on iron, they are gonna give you a generic iron pill, rather than trying to see WHY is your iron low. Is it low intake? Or do you have an absorption problem? Is there a gut or digestive issue? If they are good they will at least check for internal bleeding and ask about menstruation, but that’s about it. Everything is looked at with a reductionist, absolutist, universalist mindset. 

And why wouldn’t they be? Not a lot of time in a 15 minute office visit to debug someone’s lipid metabolism or troubleshoot their RAAS system pathways to get to the root cause of their health issues…. 

We need diagnostics that can accurately assess nutrition, the health of various systems and metabolic pathways, gene expression, etc, so we can see what exactly is going on with an individual’s body given their lifestyle and genome and inputs. Don’t just say “drink less alcohol, alcohol is bad for you” (and DEFINITELY don’t say “be sure you drink a glass or two of red wine with dinner for heart health!). Say “based on X, Y, and Z testing your body is handling your alcohol intake pretty well, though we should also do some regular liver screenings”.

This is not medicine; it’s PUBLIC HEALTH. And it’s based on the potentially false assumption that all of us are basically the same or that any differences average out. They don’t seem to allow for the possibility that what might be a very healthy diet for one person might be disastrous for someone else. They don’t seem to appreciate how interconnected things like diet and lifestyle are and how many complex dependencies and relationships there are. The advice we give is just … bad. Because it’s all generality. 

We should be screening people for signs of atherosclerosis, and once signs show up, troubleshooting what is going on with THAT person, rather than just a generic protocol they prescribe for all patients. We should be looking at not just bio markers, but genetics, Epigenetics, and looking for better diagnostics that can help ascertain what is actually going on in the body. Instead of telling someone to eat a low salt diet for hypertension, how about actually finding what is causing the hypertension in that person, and then basing treatment on targeting those systems. 

We already know that nutritionism is broken at the philosophical level. For some people, they can’t convert certain forms of nutrients to active forms efficiently (folic acid methylation, for example, or converting beta carotene to vitamin A)… yet our nutritional advice does not account for these types of things. If you’re low on iron, they are gonna give you a generic iron pill, rather than trying to see WHY is your iron low. Is it low intake? Or do you have an absorption problem? Is there a gut or digestive issue? If they are good they will at least check for internal bleeding and ask about menstruation, but that’s about it. Everything is looked at with a reductionist, absolutist, universalist mindset. 

And why wouldn’t they be? Not a lot of time in a 15 minute office visit to debug someone’s lipid metabolism or troubleshoot their RAAS system pathways to get to the root cause of their health issues…. 

We need diagnostics that can accurately assess nutrition, the health of various systems and metabolic pathways, gene expression, etc, so we can see what exactly is going on with an individual’s body given their lifestyle and genome and inputs. Don’t just say “drink less alcohol, alcohol is bad for you” (and DEFINITELY don’t say “be sure you drink a glass or two of red wine with dinner for heart health!). Say “based on X, Y, and Z testing your body is handling your alcohol intake pretty well, though we should also do some regular liver screenings”.

positive.text: I have made some good changes since October first of 2025. At 65, I wanted to try something new. I stopped eating rice, pasta, and potatoes. ### Summary: Boost Brain Autophagy for Mental Clarity

**Core Concept:** Brain autophagy is a distinct cleaning process that removes dysfunctional components from neurons, resulting in mental clarity, focus, and reduced brain fog.

---

### 1. What is Brain Autophagy?
- **The Process:** Cellular cleanup specifically within brain neurons, clearing out old, decaying parts that create "exhaust" (oxidative stress).
- **The Feeling:** Mental consolidation, laser focus, and reduced brain fog. It feels like "slow is smooth, smooth is fast."

### 2. How to Induce Brain Autophagy
- **Fasting:** Even short fasts (e.g., 16 hours) trigger significant neuronal autophagy.
- **Ketones:** Cleaner-burning fuel for the brain that reduces oxidative stress. Can be elevated by exercise or MCT oil, even without a strict keto diet.
- **Key Supplements:**
    - **Glutamine:** Crucial for the Glutamate (focus) / GABA (calm) cycle. Deficiency leads to a "wired but tired" brain. Essential for precision focus during a fast.
    - **Spermidine:** Directly promotes neuronal autophagy. Found in wheat germ, mushrooms, aged cheeses.
    - **Urolithin A:** Specifically targets **mitophagy**—cleaning mitochondria in the energy-demanding brain.
    - **Theanine:** Promotes calm and crosses the blood-brain barrier to locally inhibit mTOR.

### 3. Autophagy in the Body & Other Methods
- **Stacking Stressors:** Exercise induces **3x more autophagy** than fasting. Combine them (fasted exercise) for maximum effect.
- **Hormonal Help (Ghrelin):** The "hunger hormone" signals autophagy. Coffee or green tea with cinnamon can **mask hunger pangs** without lowering beneficial ghrelin levels.
- **Fasting-Mimicking Protocols:**
    - **Olive Oil Fast:** Consume 1-2 tbsp of high-quality olive oil every 4-6 hours. The antioxidants (oleopein) trigger autophagic flux while keeping insulin low.
    - **MCT Oil Fast:** Same protocol. Provides clean ketones for the brain and improves neural network stability.

### 4. Action Plan & Homework
- **The Goal:** Combine regular fasting with targeted supplements (Glutamine, Urolithin A, Spermidine) and lifestyle factors (exercise, cold, sauna).
- **Immediate Task:** Start with inexpensive **glutamine** and a short fast to experience the cognitive benefits.

positive.author: @BudKash
positive.text:
Hold on a second, Doc. I was under the impression that, although K2 is essential for D3 functionality, when taken together (as in a compound pill) they tend to conflict, because they compete for receptors. Have you heard this, and what is your opinion? I thought it's best to take D with Magnesium, but in terms of other co-factors, Zinc should not be taken simultaneously with Mag either, for instance.
You mentioned "mega-dosing", and this idea of doctors putting a patient on 50k iu daily for a brief period. Is it not true that D3 need to build up to the recommended blood levels, and to expedite this process it helps to take larger doses, especially if it was reduced to a maintenance dose thereafter? Some companies also market high-dose vit D, one brand specifically packages 50k iu caps, but as a weekly dosage, which seems reasonable if it takes time to accumulate and distribute. USRDA's are a bad joke.
All that being said, there are other important co-factors as well, especially for higher dosages of D3 (which your 10k iu daily could be considered) such as zinc, boron, vit A (beta carotene), and preferably a good B-complex also (like a methylated compound).

positive.text: As a cardiovascular health specialist, I can say this video highlights a method that is often overlooked but strongly supported by clinical research. Techniques like this can activate the nervous system in a way that rapidly lowers blood pressure, sometimes more effectively than traditional aerobic exercise when done correctly. The key is consistency and proper technique. This is a safe, practical approach that many patients can start using immediately alongside medical guidance.

transcript.summary: The speaker discusses the importance of tracking bone health in real-time, highlighting the limitations of traditional DEXA imaging and the benefits of using bone turnover markers.

positive.author: @dixiecrane1
positive.text: I am grateful that you are focusing on this challenging topic. It is discouraging to be treated by professionals who are not highly educated on bone density; they simply use a DEXA scan, then prescribe Calcium supplements plus a standard medication. I had to educate my oncologist about the need for D3 + K2. She googled it right while I was in her office and was surprised. (I learned about it from you!) I also got a vibration plate. My last DEXA showed I was back in the Osteopenia range. I'll keep doing it my way, thank you!
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @lauragrady3227
positive.text: Dr. Doug, I have started using Function Health testing to manage my overall health proactively.  These two bone turnover tests are not currently offered as an add on test. I have requested these be added.  Thanks for all your videos!  I appreciate all the valuable information you provide.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @franrushie.510
positive.text: I will be 78 this year… a few years ago with a DEXA scan I was told my spine had a score of -4 and my hip had a score of -2… the doctors wanted to put me on medication…I told them I don’t take medication made with chemicals…I told the doctors I will look for natural remedies…I started an aggressive exercise program.. plus I switched to a meat, chicken, 🍗 fish, dairy diet…. I have had 3 fall since then to where my hip had a black and blue bruise and no broken bones..
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @susanc5314
positive.text: New here...68yo, diagnosed with osteoporosis in 2024. Under pressure I took alendronate for four months, then stopped. Started collagen daily, upped protein, severely lowered carbs, stopped my 1-a-day diet soda. I've eaten mostly whole foods for decades. I exercise although not always consistent. Had a follow up visit yesterday and my endocrinologist chastised me refusing to take more medication. She prescribed a new Dexa scan (which I'll do), bloodwork, and wants me to take Reclast as the side effects of the alendronate was part of my refusal to continue. Thank you for the video, now I know I can make improvements to bone density without meds. Wish I could find a better doctor.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @riarivers-hilton7985
positive.text: For more proper testings with trials we need more scientists (you know what I mean) and money!
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @acem9302
positive.text: Dr. Doug. Thanks you very much for all the valuable info you are willing to share. For anybody else interested,  I got a doctor to order the lab tests and for the first time I am submitting them to my insurance. According to LabCorp the cost (with no insurance) is $190 for CTX and $274 for P1NP.  In the past I got them both through an online place for $225. Maybe it is wishful thinking but I am hoping my insurance will help me get a lower cost than the $225. Worst case scenario it will go towards my deductible.
positive.label: Positive

negative.author: @charlottejohnk6712
negative.text: My GP wanted me to take Fosamax but when she laughed at me when I told her I have lifted heavy weights for 40 years and she said lifting weights doesn’t help bones!   (I have a degree in exercise science) I decided although she’s very sweet osteoporosis isn’t her forte.   I then went to an endocrinologist and he put me on Fosamax and assured me that I would tolerate it and I would have a fabulous outcome.  I have never had joint pain.  Within 6 weeks I couldn’t bend forward because of horrible knee pain, my metatarsals were in horrible pain and I started having severe jaw pain.  I stopped taking Fosamax and will never take it again.  Needless to say, I am so glad that I found you!
negative.label: Negative

transcript.summary: The video discusses the science behind sleep and fasting, presenting a positive and empowering message about understanding and working with one's biology.

highlightTokens.token: You're not crazy, and you're not alone.
Once you understand these mechanisms, you can work with them, not against them.
Sleeplessness isn't always a red flag.
Sometimes it's a sign your body is activating its most ancient survival systems instead of panicking over a few restless nights.

positive.author: @HealthMetabolicScience
positive.text:
If you’ve ever fasted and found yourself wide awake at 2–3 a.m., read this before panicking.

You’re not losing sleep because you’re hungry.
👉 You’re awake because your brain has switched into survival mode.

Without food, the brain increases orexin, cortisol, and adrenaline to keep you alert — just like our ancestors who stayed awake to hunt, not to sleep.
So feeling wired while fasting isn’t a mistake — it’s ancient biology doing its job.

The real question isn’t “Why can’t I sleep?”
👉 It’s “How do I work with my biology instead of fighting it?”

👉 When you fast, do you usually sleep less but feel sharper, or feel restless and anxious at night?
Share your experience below — you’re not alone.

positive.author: @ytpah9823
positive.text:
🎯 Key points for quick navigation:

💡 Controlling insulin, the "master hormone" regulating fat storage, is key to improving diet outcomes and overall energy.
🧠 Brain fog, stubborn body fat, and energy fluctuations may be linked to a single master hormone: insulin.
⚠️ Insulin management is crucial even for lean, fit, and healthy individuals, as silent struggles can rob energy and focus.
🗺️ The video will cover four key areas: how insulin works, a mineral to "turn off" insulin resistance, how a small amount of sugar can control glucose spikes, and an actionable timeline.
⚖️ Insulin is necessary but is also the "absorptive hormone" that helps absorb both glucose and fat, which can be problematic if not managed.
🛡️ Controlling insulin spikes is essential for proper nutrient absorption, glucose entering the muscle for energy, and preventing unnecessary fat storage.
🚫 Insulin stops fat loss by turning off hormone-sensitive lipase, keeping the body in an "absorptive mode" where stored fat cannot be released into the bloodstream.
🍽️ Periods of absorption are necessary for nutrients, but too much absorption can stress the body, cause excess inflammation, and lead to feeling unwell.
🛑 Too much insulin becomes inflammatory, promotes fat storage, causes "brain fogging," and can halt mitochondria from producing energy.
🥛 Calcium, typically associated with bones and teeth, plays an arguably more critical role in metabolism.
🚨 Calcium acts as the "go signal" or trigger that causes the pancreas's beta cells to release insulin into the bloodstream when blood sugar rises.
🔬 The rush of calcium into the cell is the physical trigger that initiates insulin release, a mechanism confirmed by molecular data.
✅ Supporting the initial calcium mechanism can lead to more efficient insulin release, allowing glucose to clear faster without the pancreas overworking.
💧 A simple takeaway is to sip on high-calcium mineral water (like Gerolsteiner or San Pellegrino) or consume A2 milk or Kefir throughout the day.
🍶 Kefir is recommended because it provides calcium along with the benefits of probiotics and fermented food.
💊 Adding calcium supplements should be avoided unless a specific need is identified, as they can increase coronary artery calcium and are not recommended by groups like the American Heart Association.
🐟 Getting calcium from food sources like sardines (with bone), Kefir, and cottage cheese is preferred over supplements.
💪 The "ultimate insulin hack" that doesn't require supplements or fancy food is muscle contractions—simply moving your body.
🏃 Muscle contraction, through movement like bodyweight squats, push-ups, or even a walk, can pull glucose out of the bloodstream without requiring insulin.
🚪 Your muscles have GLUT4 transporters (glucose gateways) that typically wait for insulin to open them, but muscle contraction bypasses this.
🔥 Contracting a muscle activates the energy sensor AMPK, which signals the GLUT4 gateways to immediately move to the cell surface and let glucose in for fuel, bypassing the need for insulin.
🚶 The easiest application is to move (e.g., 10-20 push-ups or a 10-15 minute walk) immediately after a meal instead of sitting down.
🎯 Immediate post-meal movement pulls sugar into muscles for fuel, preventing it from spiking insulin and interfering with fat burning.
🤯 Consuming a specific, small dose of the sugar fructose can surprisingly help manage overall blood sugar response.
📉 Adding just 7.5 grams of fructose (less than a tablespoon of honey) to a glucose drink resulted in a 14% lower blood sugar response in adults with Type 2 diabetes.
🌊 This mechanism works by leveraging the liver's function: the small dose of fructose activates the enzyme hepatic glucokinase, which pre-primes the liver to aggressively pull glucose out of the blood and store it.
🍓 A small handful of berries is an ideal way to implement this, as they provide the specific dose of fructose to prime the liver, along with fiber to slow absorption and polyphenols that also affect blood sugar.
⏱️ The fructose trick is an acute strategy, not an all-day practice; take one teaspoon of raw honey or a small handful of berries 15-20 minutes before a planned high-carb meal.
🍯 This small fructose dose pre-primes the liver to buffer the coming glucose hit from the high-carb meal.
✨ Manuka honey (specifically Manukora brand) is highlighted as a potent source of quality fructose, with added antimicrobial benefits due to a high MGO content.
🔬 The amino acid glycine offers a long-term approach to blood sugar management by building a stronger, more resilient system.
📈 A study showed that glycine acts as a signal to the pancreas to build more insulin-creating beta cells, potentially increasing their amount by 80% to 130%.
🏭 Glycine "invests in the factory" by building new "assembly lines" (beta cells) via the P13K and mTORC1 pathways, increasing the pancreas's reserve capacity.
🛡️ Increased beta cell reserve capacity gives the body more "horsepower" to effectively manage metabolic stress from a bad night's sleep or a cheat meal.
❄️ Cold exposure enhances glucose uptake in muscles, primarily due to the activation of brown adipose tissue (BAT).
🤎 Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is a special fat that activates when cold to burn fuel and create heat; its favorite fuel is glucose.
🛁 A cold shower makes your brown adipose tissue "suck" glucose out of your bloodstream to fuel its heat production.
⏰ Circadian timing is the final piece of the plan, as the body's machinery and insulin sensitivity are different in the morning versus the evening.
☀️ A study found that people who ate a higher proportion of calories and carbs earlier in the day had significantly better insulin sensitivity.
⬆️ Insulin receptors are naturally more sensitive in the morning and become more resistant as the day progresses because the body is designed to handle fuel while active.
🔄 If you are metabolically unhealthy, it is better to keep carbs low in the morning to capitalize on insulin sensitivity and tap into fat storage.
🌙 Metabolically unhealthy individuals may benefit from keeping carbs low all day and having some at night, which can help align circadian rhythms and potentially improve sleep.
🚶 A recommended start to the day is a 15-20 minute walk in sunlight, combining muscle contraction with resetting the circadian rhythm.
🏋️ The ideal time to have carbohydrates is during a workout (e.g., sipping watermelon juice), as exercise uses muscle contractions to absorb glucose without needing insulin.
🫐 To reset metabolism, keep carbohydrates low but include a small amount of polyphenols (e.g., a handful of blueberries with Greek yogurt) for overall insulin management.
⏰ The fructose primer (tiny bit of honey or raspberries) should be consumed 15-20 minutes before the largest meal, particularly if that meal includes carbohydrates.
💊 Mixing 3 to 5 grams of glycine powder into a small glass before the high-carb meal can also help prime the pancreas.
🌙 Immediately after the higher-carbohydrate dinner, go for another 10-15 minute walk to use muscle contraction to dispose of glucose into the cells.
🚿 End the day with a 30-60 second cold shower to activate glucose-hungry brown fat, potentially burning more fat overnight and programming mitochondria.
🔑 Stacking these principles allows you to architect your own energy and gain control over the master hormone insulin, instead of being a victim of blood sugar fluctuations.
💡 Individuals have incredible control over insulin and are not simply at the mercy of the food they eat; simple tweaks can influence how the hormone works.
📺 The speaker recommends watching another video on how he personally got rid of his insulin resistance and kept it away for over 13 years.

positive.author: @drjazz777
positive.text:
🎯 Key points for quick navigation:

00:02 *🧪 The study challenges standard sports nutrition by testing high-carb vs very low-carb pre-exercise meals for performance.*
00:43 *🏃‍♂️ Focus on real-world middle distances: controlled 5K and 10K performance trials.*
01:12 *🎛️ Researchers tightly controlled confounders and compared a very low-carb meal to a guideline-style high-carb meal right before exercise.*
01:52:00 *🧬 Contrary to dogma, recommended carb intakes (e.g., 60–120 g/h) didn’t show the expected performance edge when variables were controlled.*
02:07:00 *🔁 Randomized crossover design: each subject did time trials on both pre-exercise meal conditions.*
02:46:00 *⚖️ Result: no difference in 5K/10K performance between high-carb and very low-carb pre-exercise meals.*
03:16:00 *🔥 Fuel use diverged: meals produced distinct carb vs fat oxidation profiles, yet performance was identical.*
05:19:00 *🧂 Presenter plug aside, electrolytes are suggested when fasting or cutting calories for comfort and adherence.*
06:14:00 *🎯 This was an acute pre-exercise meal test, not long-term diet—aimed at the immediate effect on performance.*
06:40:00 *🌙 Related evidence: some 5K studies show fasting doesn’t impair performance, though longer events may differ.*
09:28:00 *🧪 Prior trial: after 4 weeks keto adaptation, trained runners showed no decline in a 1-mile time trial or 6×800 m at >85% VO₂max.*
11:21:00 *🚀 Record fat burning: keto-adapted athletes oxidized >1.5 g/min (up to ~1.85 g/min) fat at high intensities—previously thought impossible.*

positive.text: A friend of mine invited me to spend Thanksgiving with her family. It was really great. No criticism, no unwinnable situations, no parental temper tantrums. After going home, I spent the rest of the weekend alone.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text:
A day or two into a visit with family, my mother says, "Someone is upset with you."
Rather than becoming anxious and asking for details, I replied, "It wouldn't be a visit home if I didn't.  I can cross that off my to-do list."

I need to remember these are why he does what he does. With patience and setting boundaries, I hope to not instantly get upset with my Dad
positive.label: Positive

negative.author: @iceyone7137
negative.text:
Tracey Marks is kindof a healthcare hero for making these videos.

If any "family" causes one discomfort then that's a toxic family that's only a family in the primitive sense of the word. So many people are cursed to be born in unwanted families, it's the biggest dice roll in life. It makes me so resentful not just for myself but for others too.

What I wish these psychologists taught more isn't only how to be resilient but how to fight. You need to fight too, even if it risks you becoming insane.
negative.label: Negative

negative.author: @dougjowdy4285
negative.text: It is not even worth the energy anymore to use these techniques to cope with the family. They are not fun to be around and will continue to act out their trauma. And it's not for me to learn to pivot/tap dance anymore when the situation has no value to me whatsoever. Detaching with love works best. And when indicated, in a loving manner be honest about my experience in response to their mindlessness. They cannot and will not accept that honesty is an act of love. If I can't be honest with someone, I'm left in a position feeling vulnerable. Both my ANS and adrenals find that to be a fools game to engaging in the mental gymnastics required in the face of people who are emotionally blind. I believe strongly in what you shared, it will help immensely in other situations.
negative.label: Negative

positive.author: @michaeldiener5053
positive.text: I agree that it is difficult to discern a benefit from supplementation, especially when you are trying different things. Going on my own experiene, curcumin (turmeric) + pepper is said to be good for arthritis, and I have found the incidents of flare-up at that thumb/wrist joint (CMC?) have been reduced, and I do feel looser in the hip joints when hiking. I also feel like I have had fewer of those "why was I going upstairs?" moments since I started taking creatine at a 10 mg level. These are both fairly low cost supplements. I also take a few others where my food tracker said I was consistently low, like fish oil, magnesium/zinc/D, and choline. I do add chia and flax to some foods like overnight oats and fruit jam, but I don't think of this as supplementation.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @MiddleSky
positive.text:
Thanks for this, I am getting more interested in lifestyle factors for healthspan. Supplements are expensive and don't really do much except for a few. 
The social aspect is a weak point for me, too so I look forward to hearing more on how you work on it. There are articles out there with topic suggestions on having deeper conversations, I think I'll look some up again so I can actually talk to a friend when we do a road trip this year, instead of just daydreaming the whole trip like I did last time. Uncomfortable, but I'll try to think of it like a muscle I'm strengthening.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @DebbiePearson-m9g
positive.text:
I have friends that don’t believe everything that I’ve told him and now you said it all in this video. I’m type two diabetic and I keep it under control.   
My numbers are usually between 95 and 105 when I get my doctor recommended labs  and my A1c is always under six. I eat eat potatoes I eat rice i eat everything the only thing that I changed when knowing about refrigeration, 24 hours, I did not know about but timing when to eat it everything I tell all my friends that are diabetics, including my brother that you can have starches you can have potatoes you can have all that just make sure you eat them before 2pm and make sure to leave the skin on them and eat them with protein and vegetables.  what I’m telling them. My blood tests that the doctor does periodically. My numbers are 95 to 105 and my A1c is always under six. I’ve been doing this my entire life. It works. I just have to remember to use the vinegar more often like they do in Europe on potatoes.

Vitamin B1, or thiamin, is a water-soluble vitamin essential for converting food into energy, supporting nerve function, muscle contraction, and heart health.

Deficiency (Beriberi): 
Causes nerve damage (neuritis), confusion, muscle weakness, and heart problems. 

Sources

Natural: Yeast, cereal grains, beans, nuts, meat (especially pork), and poultry.
Fortified: Enriched breads, cereals, and rice.
Supplements: Available individually or as part of a B-complex.

positive.author: @ThomasDeLauerOfficial
positive.text: I put together a meal plan for insulin resistance using Whole Foods, here it is for free: http://www.thomasdelauer.com/eatrealfood - The best way to adhere to something is just have a plan. This is a thank you for joining my newsletter and subscribing
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @JimsworldSanDiego
positive.text:
Read along:
Cold Plunge (0:10): Rated 4/10. Primarily beneficial for mental resilience rather than significant physiological changes like mitochondrial health or brown fat stimulation in acute settings. Prolonged exposure to moderately cool temperatures is more effective.
Sauna (1:02): Rated 9/10. High heat saunas offer substantial benefits for heat shock proteins, mitochondrial resilience, and lymphatic drainage for the brain. Infrared saunas are good, but high heat provides the most significant advantages.
High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) (1:57): Rated 10/10. Provides metabolic benefits of both resistance training and aerobic conditioning. However, it's easy to overdo, leading to increased cortisol and sleep disruption. Keep sessions under 15 minutes of total work time, a few times per week.
Zone 2 Training (2:50): Rated 7.5/10. Excellent for building the "floor" of metabolic health and improving mitochondrial efficiency, making the body more resilient and enhancing recovery.
Detoxing (3:45): Rated 5/10. True detoxification happens internally by supporting the body's natural processes with tools like soluble fiber and antioxidants. External detoxes are largely ineffective.
Fasting (4:43): Rated 8/10. Effective for fat loss, mental clarity, autophagy, and cellular cleanup. The key is not to overdo it, as it can become mere caloric restriction.
Wearables (5:56): Rated 6/10. While providing valuable metrics and data, they can cause users to lose touch with their own body's signals.
Resistance Training (7:04): Rated 10/10. Highly beneficial for brain health, metabolism, detoxification, and overall bodily function.
Creatine (7:18): Rated 9/10. Research increasingly shows its benefits extend to anti-inflammatory pathways, helping control inflammation at systemic, brain, muscular, and joint levels.
Personalized Supplements & Gene Testing (7:59): Rated 4/10. Often expensive and not always necessary, as many people need similar basic supplements. Genetic testing can be useful for specific mutations but doesn't provide a complete health picture.
Blue Light Blocking Glasses (9:11): Rated 6/10. While blue light at night isn't ideal, reducing overall brightness and avoiding LED flicker (by switching to incandescent lights) are more crucial for brain health and sleep.
Kiwi for Sleep (10:09): Rated 3/10. Despite containing melatonin-boosting properties, kiwis are high in glucose, which can disrupt sleep for many, counteracting any potential benefits.
Raw Milk (11:02): Rated 6/10. While potentially beneficial in its purest form, mass production and lack of standardization make it risky due to potential contamination. A2 variety milk is a safer and good quality alternative.
Protein Everything (12:18): Rated 6/10. Protein-spiked foods can be good if they use quality protein sources like whey or milk protein. However, many products use minimal or less effective proteins for marketing purposes, so reading labels is essential.
Methylene Blue (13:04): Rated 8/10. Highly effective for strategic, low-dose use during periods of stress, high altitude, or increased training volume, aiding mitochondrial function and recovery. Not recommended for daily use.
Peptides (13:59): Rated 5/10. Some peptides like BPC 157 and TB500 are highly beneficial, but many others are ineffective or carry more risk than reward. Thorough research is advised.
Long-Term Keto (14:55): Rated 7/10. Can lead to oxidative stress if sustained for too long.
Intermittent Keto (15:05): Rated 9.5/10. Cyclical keto (e.g., seasonal) is highly effective for brain signaling, anti-inflammatory pathways, mitochondrial biogenesis, and autophagy, making the body more resilient.
Limiting Seed Oils (15:44): Rated 7/10. Avoiding or limiting industrialized, highly processed seed oils is beneficial due to their oxidative and chemical nature. Natural sources of mono and polyunsaturated fats are fine.
positive.label: Positive

A retired educator, I found this gem an extraordinary tool to share with my grandchildren. Handled tenderly, rather than fear, I will use this to build hope and a vision of possibility for my three young teens to gird themselves with in their lives. With two of the three destined for futures in the sciences, whetting their appetites for possibilities to  be created may well prepare them to shift the zeitgeist in the generations coming.  With compassion, kindness and rigor, I have every faith that humanity, in all its imperfections, can create imperfect but perfectible opportunities to adapt and overcome the effects of climate change.  At some profound level I find the human spirit irrepressible, conundrums, parchocialisms and fear notwithstanding!

positive.text:
Short Summary:

REMOVE
1. Artificial Sweeteners
2. Ultra Processed Foods
3. Seed Oils
4. Chronic Under-eating
5. Eating in a stressed state

RESTORE
1. Repair the gut lining
- Collagen & gelatin rich foods (Bone broth, slow-cooked meats, oxtail, shanks, connective tissue...)
2. Reintroduce beneficial bacteria (Sauerkraut, Kefir, Yogurt, Kimchi)
3. Support digestion
- proper chewing
- warm foods over cold
- (Apple cider vinegar)

REGULATION
1. Consistent meal timing
- Regular eating windows
- No constant grazing

2. Parasympathetic dominance
- Sit down to eat
- No phone
- No meetings
- No rushing
- Calm eating beats perfect macros.

3. Circadian alignment
- Morning light
- Earlier dinners
- Better sleep = better gut repair

4. Stress management
- Walks
- Nature
- Sauna
- Breathwork

positive.author: @guthealer1
positive.text:
Lucas hit the nail on the head at 8:27 about how eating in a stressed state completely shuts down digestion. That was a massive lightbulb moment for me.

However, for anyone watching who has severe IBS or a highly damaged gut, be very careful with the raw arugula/salad advice at 12:12! When my gut was at its absolute worst, eating raw greens to 'kickstart' digestion literally acted like sandpaper on my inflamed stomach and made me look 6 months pregnant instantly.

Before I could tolerate raw greens or salads again, I had to apply 'Mechanical Rest' to my meals. I temporarily stopped all raw veggies and cooked everything down to absolute mush or purees. By taking the physical breakdown work away from my stomach, my gut finally had the mechanical peace it needed to heal and actually absorb things like bone broth. You have to remove the physical friction before your gut can handle raw greens! Spot on video overall, especially the stress management.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text:
I’ve been battling obesity most of my life, peaking at 395 lbs. I fought my way down to 250, but for years I’ve been in a tug-of-war between 250 and 300. When life hits hard—like losing my sister to cancer—my mental health takes a beating and I lose my rhythm.

When I’m on carnivore or fasting, my body screams for water. But in a downward spiral? I lose that thirst signal and reach for the 'tasty' stuff that I know is bad for me. I’m subscribed because your research helps me get back on track every time I’m in survival mode.

Also, as a student of content creation myself, I have a new appreciation for what you do! The research alone must take half your day. Thanks for the info—it’s the little steps like this that help me keep fighting.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text:
Great, thanks all. Summary.
Explains how UVB, red, and near‑infrared light act as biological signals that regulate hormones, immunity, circadian rhythms, and cellular energy. It highlights how different wavelengths interact with the skin, eyes, and brain to influence health across the lifespan.

🌞 UVB Light and Hormonal / Immune Activation
UVB light from sunlight triggers major physiological responses. When UVB hits the skin, it increases production of testosterone and estrogen, improves mood, and stimulates stem cell turnover that supports healthier skin, hair, and nails. When UVB reaches the eyes, it activates a neural pathway to the spleen, prompting the release of immune cells such as T‑cells and B‑cells, effectively placing the body in a heightened defensive state. UVB exposure also increases endogenous opioids like beta‑endorphins, raising pain tolerance and contributing to feelings of well‑being.

🌙 Light, Melatonin, and the Circadian Clock
Light regulates the body’s internal timing system through the pineal gland and melatonin. Melatonin acts as a seasonal “calendar,” with higher levels in winter influencing bone density and puberty timing. Exposure to bright light—especially UVB or blue light—between 10 p.m. and 4 a.m. sharply suppresses melatonin and activates a brain region that reduces dopamine, increasing vulnerability to depression. Maintaining darkness or dim red light at night protects circadian stability.

🔴 Red and Near‑Infrared Light for Cellular Repair
Long‑wavelength red (670 nm) and near‑infrared (790 nm) light penetrate deeply into tissues and directly affect mitochondria, increasing ATP production while reducing harmful reactive oxygen species. Research from Dr. Glen Jeffery shows that viewing red light for 2–3 minutes in the early morning can improve visual acuity by about 22% in adults over 40 by restoring energy to aging photoreceptors and reducing drusen. Red light also accelerates wound healing and supports acne treatment by activating dermal stem cells. Dr Jeffery consulted on the development of our glasses.

🧭 Practical Protocols
Recommended practices include 20–30 minutes of sunlight exposure several times weekly, using red light therapy only in the morning, and relying on dim red light at night—especially for shift workers. Individuals with conditions such as glaucoma, macular degeneration, or skin cancer risk should consult specialists before increasing UVB exposure.

negative.author: @johanneshalberstadt
negative.text: 06:45 Also: too little choline in the brain, may not have to do with how much you eat. You can eat enough, or more than enough, choline and still have less available in the brain, because after eating -like all nutrients- it has to pass the intestinal wall first, which can already be impaired or facilitated in different people. Then it goes from your intestines into your blood, where special vessels take it to your liver first, then there is processing in the liver, before it even goes into your general blood stream, and once it is there, it still needs to pass the blood-brain-barrier and needs to end up exactly where it is needed in the brain. That means that there are multiple steps and mechanisms that don't have to do with your take-in, that could determine how much is available in your brain. And also the transformation of choline into acetyl choline may be much more determined by the availability and activity of specialized anzymes that tramsfom it, rather than just enough choline being there. As an analogy: of you have to few builders to build your house (the enzymes), giving them more bricks (choline) does not get your house built faster. You need more workers. This is, in my opinion, a fundamental mosunderstanding that people have regarding mamy things to do with nutrition. Often times it is not the supply of raw materials (nutrients) that determines a desired outcome, but your internal machinery. Now people temd to feel like giving your body more of a certain raw material would somehow "tell your body" to make more of the endproduct. But thats just not how it works. Your enzymes amd cells arent sentient conscious beings capable of symbolic communication. I believe people tend to think that if they give more of a certain starting material, your body would then "understand" that that "means" yoou want it to make more of a certain endproduct. But giving more of the starting material is not what triggers higher productivity. It just means there is enough there if and when mechanisma are kicked into action. Bit what kicks them into action is dependet on your bodys internal regulatory control loops, not on presence or absence of starting materials.
negative.label: Negative

positive.text: I'm an old athlete, emphasis on old ...  All of us who have tried to maintain physical capability across a lifespan know that "something is better than nothing".   You do not need to be achieving "optimum heart rate" nor "fat burning".  You do need to exercise in ways that do more good than harm.  As we age, low impact aerobics, lighter weights, and a sensible diet are needed so you don't damage your body beyond its ability to rebuild. positive.author: @TomGuard
positive.text:
Here is a bulleted summary of the video "Neuroscientist Reveals Diet that Doubles Autophagy More than Fasting":
​Modified Fasting for Autophagy: The video discusses a diet strategy that induces autophagy more effectively than a complete fast. This involves a "modified fasting" or modified ketogenic diet approach [00:30], [00:44].
​The Protocol: This method requires creating a significant energy deficit for a period of 3 to 5 days, aiming for about 500 calories per day [01:05], [08:52]. This is done periodically, such as once every one to three months [01:20].
​Therapeutic Ketosis: The goal is to lower blood glucose and elevate ketones, achieving a state of "therapeutic ketosis," which is correlated with markers of autophagy [00:52], [01:27].
​Cardiometabolic Benefits: This periodic protocol can lead to long-term improvements in cardiometabolic biomarkers, including triglycerides, blood glucose, and fasting insulin, even after resuming a normal diet. It is particularly beneficial for those with insulin resistance [01:37], [02:12].
​Key Drivers: The primary driver of this effect is the energy deficit [04:35], [10:47]. A ketogenic state (by restricting carbohydrates) amplifies the process by suppressing insulin, which stimulates "autophagic flux" [06:25], [06:52].
​Stacking with Exercise: Exercise is described as one of the biggest levers for inducing autophagy [04:56]. Even light exercise, like a brisk walk, can be "stacked" with the diet to magnify the autophagic response [05:07].
​Duration: A 3-to-5-day period is recommended. The guest notes that fasting beyond five days can start to negatively impact hormones [07:44], [08:04].
​Behavioral Benefits: This modified approach is often more behaviorally sustainable than a complete water fast [10:23]. It helps "train" the body and mind, potentially improving one's long-term relationship with food and preventing the urge to binge afterward [14:51].
​Gut Health: Giving the digestive system a rest with this low-calorie period can also help improve gut barrier function [21:36], [44:41].
​Foods Mentioned for Autophagy
​The video emphasizes a dietary pattern (calorie restriction + carbohydrate restriction) rather than specific "autophagy-boosting" foods. The foods mentioned are suggested as nutrient-dense options to consume within the 500-calorie limit to provide essential fatty acids and amino acids, which helps preserve muscle mass [11:58].
​Foods mentioned in this context include:
​Sardines [11:41], [20:31]
​Mackerel [20:31]
​Fish (in general) [11:48]
​Egg yolks [11:48]
​Liver [11:48]
​Broccoli [20:59]
​Additionally, coconut oil was mentioned for its lauric acid content, which has antimicrobial properties that can help lower inflammation from underlying infections [51:03], [51:17].
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @Bethesda-angel
positive.text:
Key Points
	1.	What is autophagy?
Autophagy is a cellular “self-cleaning” process where damaged or dysfunctional components inside cells are recycled, helping maintain cellular health.  ￼
	2.	Why it matters
The video argues that boosting autophagy may help with longevity, better metabolic health, and improved cellular repair. Also implicates upstream processes (e.g., nutrient sensing, fasting) in triggering it.
	3.	The main claim
The video suggests there’s a dietary approach that doubles autophagy compared to standard fasting protocols. (Note: the exact protocol is presented in the video.)
	4.	What the dietary approach involves
According to the video (and companion commentary), the approach emphasizes calorie reduction or a fasting-mimicking diet, rather than simply skipping meals or traditional fasting. Some comments mention a ~500-calorie method.  ￼
It draws on research showing that calorie restriction or intermittent fasting can increase autophagy markers.  ￼
	5.	Mechanisms discussed
	•	Lower nutrient/energy availability → triggers nutrient-sensing pathways (e.g., mTOR inhibition, AMPK activation) → induces autophagy.
	•	The diet or fasting triggers a ‘metabolic switch’ (e.g., from glucose to fat/ketones) which also promotes autophagy and cellular repair.
	•	The video emphasizes that simply skipping meals may not be as effective as the controlled dietary strategy being highlighted.
	6.	Practical aspects / recommendations
	•	The video suggests implementing a periodic low-calorie phase rather than constant severe restriction.
	•	It likely recommends pairing the dietary strategy with healthy baseline habits (exercise, good sleep).
	•	It warns that this kind of approach may not be suitable for everyone (especially those with health conditions) and that the research is still emerging.
	7.	Caveats and limitations
	•	Much of the supporting research comes from animal models or small human studies; human evidence is less robust.
	•	“Doubling” autophagy is a bold claim; how this translates into long-term health benefits remains to be fully demonstrated.
	•	Individual responses vary; what works for one person may not for another.
	•	Safety is stressed: such approaches require oversight if applied in vulnerable populations.

⸻

🔍 My Assessment & Take-aways
	•	The video conveys an interesting idea: that a tailored dietary approach (not just fasting) might more powerfully activate autophagy.
	•	This could be relevant if you’re exploring health optimisation or longevity strategies—but it’s not a proven “miracle”.
	•	If you’re considering applying something like this:
	•	Make sure you’re medically cleared (especially if you have metabolic, endocrine, or eating-disorder concerns).
	•	Use it as one tool among others (nutrition + exercise + sleep + stress).
	•	Recognise that results and safety will depend on individual context.
	•	Because you asked for a summary, I want to emphasise: I didn’t find strong independent verification of the exact “doubles autophagy” figure in high-quality human trials from quick searches—so treat that claim cautiously.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @androSS.
positive.text:
I have severe plaque psoriasis that at one point growing up, probably covered about 85% of my body. I went through photo light therapy, dermalogic injections and immunosuppressive medications. I’ve gone through the gamut of trying to find a resolution to this as at its worst, can transition to psoriatic arthritis and effect my joints.

I had stumbled upon your channel, some 9 years ago and I started intermittent fasting and getting back to working out. My initial thought was that psoriasis seems to be an overproduction of cells - which then tricks the body into a response that ends up making my skin react to that response. Through various studies, it has shown that irritation and or the source, could be directly tied to gut health. So I figured, what if autophagy and fasting can reverse this “wild production of cells” that’s effecting my skin?  

I now IF anywhere from 4-5 days a week avg’ing about 19 hours with just water, black coffee or green tea. I utilize pink Himalayan salt for the minerals and I still take my multivitamins and supplements to assist throughout the days… and I’ve never felt better physically, mentally and spiritually. 

While I’m not completely psoriasis free and still need the help of a biologic medication.. I have never felt more confident to wear shorts or go to the pool. I feel like IF really has allowed my body to act as optimally as possible under my current circumstances. 

Also, I’m a nurse and work 13 hr shifts. I’ll fast during those days and bust out 5.5-6 miles a shift on average. I rarely if ever have brain fog or endurance issues. I break my fast with either a protein shake or some collagen and allow myself to digest that. I’ll then eat my “first meal” about an hour or so after. 

IF has changed my life and a lot of fasting “properly” came with your insight and videos. 

I’ll take a gander at this alternate form and try to give it a shot. 

Thanks dude! Blessings.

positive.text: Good and informative video… however… there was a lot of repetition and there is conflicting info… I do intermittent fasting (16hrs fasting 8hr eating window) and I skip breakfast and finish dinner by 7/7.30pm at the latest… skipping breakfast is more sustainable (in the long term) than skipping dinner… i’ve also incorporated exercise (running/walking and gym) and have a lost a lot of weight (at a steady pace)… and have felt more healthy, have a lot more concentration, have better sleep etc… weight loss, insulin resistance etc varies between person to person… and to see results with weight loss… you need to be in a calorie deficit - i.e. eat less but also have a healthy and balanced diet during your eating window… by doing this and incorporating my workouts… I have managed to lose weight and have a healthier life
positive.label: Positive

Questions:  How many exercises should one do in each of these areas? when does it become over kill to the point of limited returns (risking injury). If you only have 2 hours to work on legs...what's the best mix? - for example 50% quads, 30% hams, 20% calfs/glutes.  Currently, this is what I'm doing... mainly high volume, lower weight as I'm 65. negative.text:
FAQ

Q: Are hormone harmony blends effective in perimenopause?
A: Usually not. They often contain too many ingredients at low doses, and some herbs like vitex may not be effective postmenopause. Focus on targeted nutrients you actually need.

Q: Should I take a multivitamin?
A: Only if you’re deficient in specific nutrients that you can’t get through food. Whole foods are preferred; supplements are for gaps or genetic limitations (e.g., vitamin D conversion issues).

Q: Are calcium supplements necessary?
A: Only if dietary intake is insufficient. Excess calcium from supplements can cause kidney stones or cardiovascular calcifications. Aim for ~1,200 mg/day, ideally from food, with vitamin D (and K2 if possible).

Q: Should I take iron supplements?
A: Only if you are iron deficient. Unnecessary iron can cause constipation, gut disruption, and other issues. Check an iron panel before supplementing.

Q: What’s the general guideline for supplementing in perimenopause?
A: Avoid generic hormone blends and unnecessary multivitamins. Supplement calcium and iron only when needed. Personalize your approach with your doctor—one-size-fits-all does not work.

positive.author: @ni1disponiblecarays
positive.text:
A trick that works for me to eat more vegetables (and for my husband to eat them too _especially that last part_) is to make a universal base for vegetable soups. I use onion, leek, celery, carrot, etc. I cook it, blend it, and freeze it in 250 g portions. When you want a vegetable soup, put the base from the container into a pot, add the vegetables you want (or any leftovers you have at home), and cook for 8 to 15 minutes. I also use a universal spice mix to season the soup. Then blend it, add cream, yogurt, or olive oil plus the toppings you like, and it’s ready. For me, 250 ml of base makes about 1 liter of soup, and it saves me a lot of time.

Another trick is to have one jar of spices for each thing (homemade).

Another one is to season salmon portions with salt and pepper, wrap them in foil, and put them in the freezer. When you want salmon, take one packet (better if you defrost it the day before, but it’s not required), put it in the air fryer for 15 minutes just like that, without unwrapping it, then open it and eat. It turns out super juicy and tender.

I also keep all kinds of bags of vegetables in the freezer and boiled eggs in the fridge, but you already said that.

1 HCL 500mg mid meal removed 80% of symptoms on week one  on week two 2 HCL and all symptoms gone finally i can enjoy food, also all my hiatal hernia symptoms gone on week two

positive.author: @johnpisano1048
positive.text:
This is simply what helped my LPR (Laryngopharyngeal reflux)  calm down — not medical advice, not a rulebook, just sharing in case it gives someone hope.
During my healing phase, I kept things very simple.
Main foods (most meals):
• Beef — ribeye, sirloin, chuck roast, ground beef (this was my base)
• Steak seemed easiest on my throat and digestion
Also included:
• Chicken — thighs, drumsticks, wings (plain, simply cooked)
• Pork — chops and loin; I avoided processed meats early on
• Eggs (when tolerated)
• Fish occasionally — salmon, sardines, white fish
Drinks:
• Water only (room temp or warm)
• Electrolytes if needed — unflavored or homemade; no citrus, sweeteners, or sugar
• No coffee, tea, alcohol, or flavored drinks during healing
What I avoided at first:
• Plant foods (vegetables, fruit, grains, beans)
• Sugar and sweeteners
• Processed meats with spices/sugars
• Sauces or seasonings beyond salt — I used salt as my only seasoning
Why I kept it simple (my personal reasoning):
Less fermentation → less gas → less abdominal pressure.
Less pressure seemed to mean less reflux mist and less throat irritation for me.
I don’t see this as forever or one-size-fits-all. Everyone’s body is different. This was just a temporary reset that seemed to give my throat a calm window to heal.
If someone feels stuck, you could consider trying something like this for about 30 days as an experiment — not a forever diet, just a short healing window to see how your body responds.

positive.text: Dr. Claire Whitmore, this video content is truly absolutely wonderful and valuable! 🤩 As a senior who frequently monitors blood pressure, I admit I made many of the basic mistakes you pointed out. positive.text: Everyone is different.  I’ve been living and competing on a low carb, high protein, moderate fat diet for over 10 years.  I’m 43 years old. I get sub-6% body fat every competition. positive.text: Something I started years ago is bi-phasic sleeping. Basically, I may sleep and then wake up 3 or 4 hours later. Instead of trying to get myself back to sleep I used to go out with my dog for an hour or so. Or these days I may read for an hour. Then I go back to sleep for maybe 2 or 3 hours. I found that that second sleep is so much more satisfying. I wake up completely rested and feel good. I started that by accident and later found out that there's evidence that people used to sleep that way. Before they had electricity, they would go to sleep early and wake up in the middle of the night and talk with their spouse or had sex or whatever. And there are old books and supposedly even the bible , that reference the first and the second sleep.

positive.text: 3rd.attemt. I am 95 years old.. I know that I have been type two diabetic for at least seven years. positive.text: Hypothesis: the "stress" of feeling stuck in some threatening situation results in Emotional Resistance, a new term I just coined. The ability to cry, for instance, is lost. Repression is systematic, such that not only is the emotional response impaired, but the fluidity between thinking and intentional and emotional centers is also diminished. This makes us both temporarily less "bothered" by our situation and less intelligent. The solution, not mentioned here, is to loosen the grip on emotional control and allow the instinct to emote to materialize. In a word, learn to cry consciously about stressful things. Try this and watch your intelligence and self direction return, along with your sense of humor.

negative.author: @robmetabolic
negative.text:
I think what happens to many - to me at least - is we get into a situation, usually a work situation, where we have little control and then this can throw us off because we are always “reacting” or we feel we are, rather than consciously responding
I was in a surgical residency. They actually told you the ideal was to be so “uptight” that a piece of coal in your butt would turn into a diamond…. It was a hazing of a sort, to make one feel powerless, perpetually scared. It was pathological, and each more senior resident (usually) behaved in a demeaning way to the residents or interns less senior to them. Rather than being supportive and nurturing - because this is what they experienced

But this is a setup for extreme stress. Yes, it will have you waking up in a cold sweat wondering if you checked that lab value, things like that - so I suppose it seems to “work”. But there’s another way. Calm, systematic processes. Haste does make waste.
And this stress environment causes a number of things
Maladaptive behaviors and people being a$$holes to each other.

It’s no wonder there are very high rates of alcohol and drug abuse, suicide and divorce in these jobs.

And actually truly ironic, when it’s supposed to be about “health”.

You must take care of the body
You must take care of the mind
You must take care of the soul

Small habits - introduce them slowly, like a couple of daily 5 min meditation breaks
Doing a set of body squats after a meal to mitigate blood glucose spike
Spending one minute doing gratitude affirmations in the morning and before sleeping 
A wind down process for bed with no devices, taking magnesium and doing Huberman’s physiologic sighs.

I used to do the Buddhist practice of Vipassana and metta meditation - But I let that slide, as well as many other good things like regular exercise, when the tidal wave of stress came over me - when you feel you have no control over your time - this is not a good or healthy situation to be in.

We are stressed when we feel we have no agency, no control, and that we are constantly fighting off threats. It is not a sustainable situation. Remember that you are important - you are worth saving, you deserve to feel health, safety and peace - or you can’t be of use to anyone.
negative.label: Negative

negative.author: @r-type4945
negative.text: The same issues are triggered by trauma. I like the intervention list, but the biggest problem I see is that most individuals don’t have the capacity to keep them up. If stress is constant, the environment stays the same, no person to guide one and the brain having lost much of its capacity for willpower and clear thinking already, I think chances are very low for a person to pull themselves out of that rut.
negative.label: Negative

neutral.text:
Hey guys, just wanted to clarify and answer a commonly asked (and important) question: IS IT SAFE TO COOL RICE AND THEN REHEAT IT?
The concern there is a bacteria called B. cereus, which can produce spores/toxins. 
The overall risk of B cereus toxin infection is extremely low from refrigerated, properly handled rice, and only arise from improper cooling or prolonged room temperature storage after cooking, or inadequate reheating. The main risk arises if rice is left at room temperature for extended periods after cooking, allowing B. cereus spores to germinate and multiply, potentially producing toxins that are not always destroyed by reheating.
So here are some general safety guidelines to minimize the risk of infection: rapid cooling and proper refrigeration is critical
- rice needs to be cooled PROMPTLY after cooking, and stored at ≤4 C  / ≤ 39 F; and then reheated thoroughly
- studies show that B cereus  growth is unlikely if rice is stored below 10C / 50 F; and in the studies I quoted in the video, it was cooled to 39 degrees F for at least 24 hrs

positive.text: I’m a registered dietitian that specializes in CSID/sucrose intolerance, and I’m SO HAPPY to see more people talking about this! positive.author: @Steve-the-Lion556
positive.text: Just some info. I've been suffering with IBS/SIBO for about 23 years, but for the first time I've managed to have a bit of a breakthrough. Some weeks ago I started using magnesium oil. In the past I've taken magnesium powder and I never noticed any improvement. So a few weeks ago I started using about 25 sprays of magnesium oil around my chest and stomach, and after a few weeks I noticed that I was having less gas. I would say my gas has reduced by about 40-50%  So I'm not cured, but I can now eat carbs without getting a huge amount of gas. It has made a big difference. What I have learned is that the vagus nerve, as well as the nerves in the intestines, are very dependant on magnesium to work properly. My next step is to supplement with thiamine (vitamin B1) as a lack of B1 can also impair the vagus nerve. But to anyone who is suffering with IBS/SIBO, try the magnesium oil.

positive.author: @DrAlexWibberley
positive.text:
Hello everyone and thank you for watching! I really hope you found this video useful. I read all of your comments and try to reply to as many as I can every day across the channel. The community on this channel is absolutely fantastic.... people sharing their stories, supporting each other, and learning together. It's amazing to see. 

It means a lot to me that this has become a space where people are interested in the simple things that keep us healthy and prevent problems before they ever reach the hospital. If there’s a topic you’d like me to explain in a future video, please let me know in the comments.

If you’d like to support me, the best thing you can do is click the like button and subscribe. It really helps these videos reach more people who might benefit from them, and it allows me to keep making them! 

My goal with these videos is simple: to help as many people as possible stay healthier and avoid ending up in the emergency department if we can. 

Wishing you all the best, and thanks again!

Dr Alex 😊
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @ThePi314Man
positive.text: Protein and exercise was never just a gym bro thing. It's literally life and longevity.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @xjet
positive.text: I'm 73 and have been resistance training for six  years (3x 10 minute workouts a week) while also walking 5-10Km a day.  I'm pharma-free.  No blood pressure meds, no blood-sugar meds, no analgesic meds.  I take a few simple supplements but nothing that is essential to my survival.   It saddens me to see so many of my peers chugging down a huge handful of pills each day when many of the conditions they suffer could be reduced or managed by simple lifestyle changes.

negative.author: @anthonybryan7191
negative.text:
The claims in that video are factually incorrect or seriously misleading. 
1) “Algae DHA is a triglyceride, so it’s harmful”
False.
A triglyceride is simply a chemical structure: 3 fatty acids attached to glycerol.
This is the normal, natural form of fats in:
Human blood
Human body fat
Most whole foods (including plants)
Key point:
Being a triglyceride does NOT make something harmful.
What matters is:
The type of fatty acid (e.g. DHA vs saturated fat)
The overall diet context
Reality:
DHA (docosahexaenoic acid) from algae is a long-chain omega-3 fatty acid
It is consistently associated with:
Reduced inflammation
Improved cardiovascular markers
Brain function support
There is no evidence that DHA triglycerides from algae increase cancer or heart disease risk.
2) “It’s as bad as fish oil or meat for heart disease, stroke, cancer”
False.
This is a conflation error.
Evidence-based distinctions:
Fish oil / algae DHA:
Generally linked to:
Lower triglycerides in blood
Slight reduction in cardiovascular risk (context dependent)
Not strongly linked to cancer risk
Meat (especially processed meat):
Associated with:
Increased risk of cardiovascular disease
Increased risk of colorectal cancer (classified by World Health Organization)
Important nuance:
Omega-3 fats (including DHA) are biologically protective, not harmful
The risk profile of meat has nothing to do with triglyceride structure
3) “DHA causes heart attacks or strokes”
False.
DHA and EPA are among the most studied fats in nutrition science
They are generally associated with:
Reduced blood triglycerides
Anti-inflammatory effects
Improved endothelial function (blood vessel health)
Clinical reality:
Some large trials show modest benefit, not harm
No credible evidence shows DHA causes cardiovascular events in healthy individuals
4) “The brain cannot absorb or use DHA”
Completely false.
This is the most incorrect claim.
Biological facts:
DHA is a major structural fat in the brain
~20–30% of the brain’s fatty acids are DHA
The brain uses DHA for:
Neuron membrane fluidity
Synapse function
Neurotransmission
Mechanism:
DHA crosses the blood-brain barrier via a transporter (MFSD2A)
Evidence:
DHA deficiency is associated with:
Cognitive decline
Poor visual development (in infants)
So the claim that the brain cannot use DHA is flatly wrong.
5) Is algae DHA different from fish DHA?
No meaningful difference in function.
Fish get DHA by eating algae
Algae oil is simply the original source
Practical advantage of algae:
No contaminants (e.g. mercury)
Vegan-compatible
Controlled DHA levels
negative.label: Negative

all.author: @anthonybryan7191
all.text:
The claims in that video are factually incorrect or seriously misleading. 
1) “Algae DHA is a triglyceride, so it’s harmful”
False.
A triglyceride is simply a chemical structure: 3 fatty acids attached to glycerol.
This is the normal, natural form of fats in:
Human blood
Human body fat
Most whole foods (including plants)
Key point:
Being a triglyceride does NOT make something harmful.
What matters is:
The type of fatty acid (e.g. DHA vs saturated fat)
The overall diet context
Reality:
DHA (docosahexaenoic acid) from algae is a long-chain omega-3 fatty acid
It is consistently associated with:
Reduced inflammation
Improved cardiovascular markers
Brain function support
There is no evidence that DHA triglycerides from algae increase cancer or heart disease risk.
2) “It’s as bad as fish oil or meat for heart disease, stroke, cancer”
False.
This is a conflation error.
Evidence-based distinctions:
Fish oil / algae DHA:
Generally linked to:
Lower triglycerides in blood
Slight reduction in cardiovascular risk (context dependent)
Not strongly linked to cancer risk
Meat (especially processed meat):
Associated with:
Increased risk of cardiovascular disease
Increased risk of colorectal cancer (classified by World Health Organization)
Important nuance:
Omega-3 fats (including DHA) are biologically protective, not harmful
The risk profile of meat has nothing to do with triglyceride structure
3) “DHA causes heart attacks or strokes”
False.
DHA and EPA are among the most studied fats in nutrition science
They are generally associated with:
Reduced blood triglycerides
Anti-inflammatory effects
Improved endothelial function (blood vessel health)
Clinical reality:
Some large trials show modest benefit, not harm
No credible evidence shows DHA causes cardiovascular events in healthy individuals
4) “The brain cannot absorb or use DHA”
Completely false.
This is the most incorrect claim.
Biological facts:
DHA is a major structural fat in the brain
~20–30% of the brain’s fatty acids are DHA
The brain uses DHA for:
Neuron membrane fluidity
Synapse function
Neurotransmission
Mechanism:
DHA crosses the blood-brain barrier via a transporter (MFSD2A)
Evidence:
DHA deficiency is associated with:
Cognitive decline
Poor visual development (in infants)
So the claim that the brain cannot use DHA is flatly wrong.
5) Is algae DHA different from fish DHA?
No meaningful difference in function.
Fish get DHA by eating algae
Algae oil is simply the original source
Practical advantage of algae:
No contaminants (e.g. mercury)
Vegan-compatible
Controlled DHA levels

These three probiotics have really helped me with leaky gut and IBS. I currently take a D-lactate–free probiotic powder (Lactobacillus rhamnosus, Lactobacillus salivarius, Bifidobacterium lactis, Bifidobacterium bifidum, Bifidobacterium infantis, Bifidobacterium longum) together with Microbiome Labs RestorFlora™ PD (Saccharomyces cerevisiae var. boulardii, Bacillus clausii, Bacillus subtilis).

 I was on a carnivore diet for about a year and a half, and I’ve now switched to a low-FODMAP diet, which continues to improve my symptoms.

After struggling with Clostridium difficile for a year, I finally recovered within one week. Saccharomyces cerevisiae var. boulardii, vancomycin, grape seed extract, and lumbrokinase enzymes made a huge difference for me — it honestly felt like a miracle.

positive.author: @ThinkScienceHD
positive.text:
Just to be very clear, this video is not saying exercise is bad or that you should stop working out. In fact, regular exercise is one of the strongest protectors of heart health.
This video exists to help people catch problems early, not to scare anyone away from a healthy lifestyle.

The goal here isn’t fear,  it’s awareness.
Train your heart. Move your body. Stay active.
But don’t rely on vibes alone. If you have risk factors or a family history, get checked and know where you stand.

positive.author: @DrAlexWibberley
positive.text:
Hello everyone and thank you for watching! I really hope you found this video useful. I read all of your comments and try to reply to as many as I can every day across the channel. The community on this channel is absolutely fantastic.... people sharing their stories, supporting each other, and learning together. It's amazing to see. 

It means a lot to me that this has become a space where people are interested in the simple things that keep us healthy and prevent problems before they ever reach the hospital. If there’s a topic you’d like me to explain in a future video, please let me know in the comments.

If you’d like to support me, the best thing you can do is click the like button and subscribe. It really helps these videos reach more people who might benefit from them, and it allows me to keep making them! 

My goal with these videos is simple: to help as many people as possible stay healthier and avoid ending up in the emergency department if we can. 

Wishing you all the best, and thanks again!

Dr Alex 😊

positive.text: I made my own kefir, sauerkraut and natto for years and eat them daily I honestly don't remember when I was sick or had a cold last time.  I have been taught to treat your food as  a medicine otherwise  medicine will become your food.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @jirislavicek9954
positive.text:
This channel is becoming S-Tier 👍
We just need to rediscover the wisdom of our ancestors and apply it to modern world. Ancestors instinctlively understood the importance of fermentation,  maturing, ripening and preservation. Asian cultures never consumed soy directly, but always in fermented form. Sauerkraut was staple food of cold climate Europe, hunters and butchers matured venison and beef to release enzymes and make the meat more digestible and tastier. Farm houses made yoghurt and cheese, wine was drink of choice for the wealthy. Fruit was dried or fermented.
People need to understand that they are part of nature and cannot isolate themselves from it and cannot exist without it. Bacteria and viruses are part of nature, both, the good and the bad ones. To be healthy means to maintain equilibrium in the body rather than obsessing about healthy diet and minimizing exposure to bacteria.

positive.author: @Alderic.
positive.text:
EXTENDED REVIEW 

Nocturne Overnight Oats:
I have finished all of them. The ‘Banana Walnut’ and ‘Blueberry’ flavors are much better than the 2 I tried in this video, unluckily enough. I want to bump it up to ‘Can Stay’ but being almost $5/ portion is a bit too steep for my SES at the moment. Will look out for sale. 

Freeze-dried Fruits & Broccoli:
Almost finished. Some of the blueberry and broccoli ended up very disintegrated perhaps because of the delivery, it became rather messy/ troublesome to eat. The peach and dragonfruit held their shape better but I prefer the flavor of the former. 

Protein Hot Cocoa:
Only had it one other time. Really kinda mid. The macros are nice though. 

Treadmill:
Working well. Previously, I was walking with socks which was how I realized the treadmill was heating up a little bit. I have since started wearing shoes. 

Chiikawa:
Still cute.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @clairez123
positive.text: For midlife women, the menopause transition has significant impact on pretty much everything. These recommendations make sense for the direct and indirect effects of estrogen decline. Autumn, making connections between recommendations and the realities of menopause would be great to increase in terms of content. Despite half the world's population will transition through menopause - literally BILLIONS of women around the world in/post menopause and most of us will live 40% of our lives in this state - menopause is significantly understudied and health care providers receive little to no training. Many women are struggling with muscle loss and central weight gain, using old techniques that simply fail because their bodies have changed - dramatically in some cases - without much to guide them how to change. Please consider more content that directly address menopause and strategies to improve health and strength. Thank you!

positive.text: I recently turned 70 and had knee surgery in the 1970s. I was always a walker but years ago switched to walking indoors. I have an open plan ranch and years ago designed an indoor course. I walk fast and for 30-50 minutes 7x a week. I recently lost 25 lbs. positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @SuzanneDoyle-i6q
positive.text: When I was a busy mom, out of shape, decided to do the ‘walk around the kitchen table’, went up and down the stairs from basement to second floor, and used kitchen food cans for working my arms. Not much…but eventually I made my way to running outside, bought used exercise equipment for my little gym in the basement. Eventually I did join a gym, hired a trainer to get a better understanding of what I should be doing. Now I’m back at my little home gym, it doesn’t take much…although hip thrust sucks without a machine, and I love the alone time to focus on me. I sometimes think I should join a gym, but love that I don’t have to worry about what I’m wearing or what I look like…and can play my own music !

Just get started

positive.author: @CidMaik
positive.text:
I do 20 - 22 hours fast with 2 hours to eat whatever I can find.
Usually walk around and do some stationary bicicle ever so often.

In between I do 48 hours (every 2 weeks) and monthly\bi monthly 72 hours. 

On weekends, just eat normally, eat whatever you want, avoid stressing about it, thinking to much about it. If you go in while stressing so much about it, cortisol rises and that is one of your number 1 enemies. 

I've been doing this for 48 days, lost 22 pounds so far. 
The first days are the roughest ones but after, not even your hunger signal bothers you. You'll understand your body better, will know the distinction of true hunger from "hey I need glucose... Give it to me" alerts you get. Slow and steady for sure when attempting this one.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @Life_style67
positive.text: It’s important to remember that every body responds differently to fasting. What works well for one person may not feel the same for someone else. In my personal experience, I’ve been practicing fasting for about seven years, and I’ve learned that mindset plays a huge role in the process. The mental shift is often more challenging than the physical aspect. The human body is actually designed to adapt; with proper hydration and electrolytes, it can function for extended periods without solid food. I once completed 28 days consuming only sugar-free squash, unsweetened almond milk, tea, and coffee. For me, the toughest part has always been the first three to four days, when hunger feels the strongest and habits are hardest to break. After that initial phase, the intense hunger usually fades, energy stabilizes, and the routine becomes much more manageable. However, fasting should always be approached carefully and with proper medical guidance.
positive.label: Positive
