positive.author: @Bill-is9lu
positive.text: I'm 72 and started berberine with keto going on 7 years ago. After my diabetes diagnosis I changed everything. I was 65 and I had neuropathy for several years. How I wasn't diagnosed with diabetes during this time or prior to this time is a question I'll always ask. But once I threw in the towel and stopped hoping that it was a mechanical issue and that different shoes would be enough I started the Burberine, in an effort, along with my diet, to lower my A1C as much as possible. I managed to go from over 9 to 5.5 in 5 months. Most of my neuropathy is gone though I wish I got to it sooner. I took berberine for probably the first 18 months pretty regularly. I've taken it sporadically in the meantime and am in fact in the middle of another meantime. Just an aside I am so much healthier than I was 12 years ago when I was 60. The mental health alone is a miracle. At 72 I'm experiencing pretty much the best health I've ever had and I found my way back to my Navy days weight. 😊
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @risingstar2758
positive.text: No matter how much medical jargon you throw at us Nick,  you make sure that the main point is conveyed and thats what i like about your videos. I take away something practical to apply in my health care journey. And thanks for the genuine effort to make the videos as simple as possble for simpletons like me who are irritated by the medical jargon...keep up the good work🤘✌
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @GrandmaMel
positive.text:
Wow! As a stage 3 cancer survivor I was told to take Anastrozole, a devastating drug for me. I stopped taking it and told my oncologist that even if not taking it shortens my life, at least I won’t be miserable.  Then I started taking berberine years ago because studies indicate that it may be a powerful anti-cancer agent. (5+ years cancer free).

My husband was placed on statins after a MI but stopped because of the side effects. I’m sharing your video with him.
I’m blown away that it also reduces insulin resistance…..studies hint that insulin resistance is a major cause of aging, dementia and other diseases….Berberine seems to be a wonder supplement!

transcript.label: Positive
transcript.summary: The video discusses the differences between anxiety and autistic overload, highlighting the importance of understanding the physiological responses of autistic individuals.

positive.author: @eledatowle8767
positive.text: When this video was recommended in my feed, I looked at the title and honestly thought, "Oh, really?  Sounds like someone trying to tell me it's all in my head," and I started the video with my arms crossed, ready for a fight.  I was completely surprised by your take on this... and comforted that we're beginning to be understood!  What you've said here is all true.  I would, however, like to add that C-PTSD has a common co-occurrence with autism, so for some of us, it's both forms, all the time.  And because of the hypervigilence AND disregulation combination, my body often reacts like we're in danger, seemingly out of the blue, even when doing something blandly enjoyable in a safe space, with no added stressors.  Once the body reacts with racing heart and the feeling of electricity running through it, no amount of rationalizing or even de-stimulating stops it, but both are part of coping with it to keep it under control. I add this only to support others like me for whom everything is a little more "complex."
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @JAYSCHULBERG-b9u
positive.text: When you mentioned the word "uncertainty", you had my full attention. Uncertainty is a major obstacle for me. A few years ago my wife and I were expecting visitors who said they would be at our home at 2:00 in the afternoon. They didn't show up until after 3:00. By the time they finally arrived, I was in no condition to do much visiting. I was completely overwhelmed by my wait and I had to excuse myself after the initial greetings. I have had similar experiences over the years, but I think that I became more susceptible to becoming overwhelmed by uncertainty since my middle 60's. Your video is very relatable. I will watch it again. Thank you!
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @itisdevonly
positive.text: This is such a good, succinct, and accurate video on the topic. All mental health professionals should have this information, because it is so important to understand when dealing with autistic clients! The strategies that help with anxiety in non-autistics can actively harm autistic people, and the last thing you want to be doing as a therapist is making the problem worse instead of helping.
positive.label: Positive

negative.author: @francoisleveille409
negative.text: If you have autism and have no help you are confronted on a daily basis to one incredible hypocrisy ; you have poor social skills, you have no help, society tells you its all in your head yet anyone at any time can exploit this weakness to cause you incredible harm. This certainly can cause a lot of anxiety.
negative.label: Negative

negative.author: @4wolves239
negative.text: "Force tends to increase fragility rather than resilience" omg yes you summed up why all my life ive been able to "push" or "force" myself to do things and instead of it making me better I just feel worse, now that im older and am aware of my needs i find myself regressing , being unable to handle things i used to and beating myself up for it , i love these videos its like you know me
negative.label: Negative

negative.author: @MentalHealthForMetalheads
negative.text: "Lack of early warnings" ...yup, that sums up why I've suddenly flipped from fine to meltdown in 2 seconds for years
negative.label: Negative

negative.author: @Larisa2005
negative.text:
Thank you for this video! 
I fully agree with your point in here. 
But I think that lack of gradual tiredness signal is the other side of constant concious putting efforts to overcome our warning system to function in the normal world at all. 
There is no interaction with chaotic behaviour and uncertainity that DOES NOT trigger autistic warning system. 
We just forcibily shut it down to force ourselves to interact with the reality at all. 
Second, about 'weak break' for alert system. It's not the case: our alert system stays 'on' because even in the quiet refuge of my flat the main stress factor never stops: chaos I was not able to cope with now is still out there. 
Many years ago I quited my job which gave me complete shutdown (to the point I stopped to understand my native language in the peak stress) and I had been living for 2 years on my savings and with my sister's help. I tried to find my next job earlier but I started to cry in a job interview. They asked really insane questions to establish authority over a possible employee. The second time I was able to work only for a week before I got nervoius chest pain and difficulty of breathing in the workplace. 
I was able to mostly collect myself in these 2 years (and I have been working for 8 years since), but forcing myself to go out in the place where I have to solve the tasks I don't personally interested about with other people who don't care about these tasks either and who don't care about the effects of their own words and actions - it's forcing myself to take part in a constant war. 
How can I relax at home if my body and mind are screaming it is insanity to keep going this way?
negative.label: Negative

neutral.text:
Speaking for myself, I have a small comfort zone and acting outside that for a long time (like at work) does wear you out.
You need to be able to spend a large part of your day back in your comfort zone to recharge.

positive.text:
I loved it when Paula said she had to trust the process when her trainer had her go from 1200 calories to 1700 cals. She had to trust it because everything she did in the past wasn't working. 

Paul Revelia's free calculator had me eating roughly 200 grams of carbs when I first started using it over a year ago but I refused to believe that could be right. I was one of those people who was always afraid of carbs so I never went above 100 grams. Anything below 100 and I never had any energy. And guess what, I never made any progress. Never lost any weight.

Six months ago I decided well maybe I should give the 200 grams a shot since nothing I did was working. And that's when I started making progress. Lost sixteen pounds in the last 4 to 5 months and it still keeps dropping as long as I remain true to the process. Thank you Paul for all your work and encouragement helping people like us!!!

positive.author: @neilgooge
positive.text:
I've said this in a previous video, but at 55 this series has finally got me in to the gym.

I have never been over weight, have always walked a considerable amount, I don't drink extensively, never smoked, and my diet has always been... okay, not amazing, but I am not a fast food or take out regularly kind of guy. All these things combined have definitely helped.  But... I could feel my strength fading, certainly in the last two to three years. Not to mentioning the increasingly stiffening joints.

And then late last year this series came along and gave me the push I needed.

What I find most incredible is... if you stood me next to your dad, let alone your mum, most people would instantly assume I could lift more... In some exercises, your mum can lift more than me, and in all cases your dad can lift more... by quite a lot in fact :D

I am genuinely excited to see where I will be a year from now, and this has truly opened my eyes to whats possible.

Thanks so so much for sharing.

One morning I finally told myself “Luise… girl… maybe stop drinking 400 calories of berries at 10 p.m. and see what happens,” and whew, the clarity that followed. My favorite time now is mid‑morning, right when I’m about to lose the will to answer another email. I’ll take one sip and suddenly I’m a functioning adult again instead of a woman negotiating with her to‑do list like it’s a hostage situation. positive.text: I’m a retired 68 year old building contractor. I’ve had 22 orthopedic surgeries. Both of my shoulders are titanium, my low back, neck and upper back are titanium with hinges and hardware. I haven’t slept on my side for years. I bought a hospital bed and it has been a blessing. I bring my legs up as high as the bed will allow and I bring my head up about 3/4. I use a cylinder shaped pillow that fits in my neck. Not too far forward or backwards. positive.text:
I have slept primarily on my right side for many decades. I’ll try sleeping on my left side. I’ll also try raising my legs for 15 minutes before going to the bed. I already tried raising my legs before bedtime to possibly reduce the frequency of waking up to urinate overnight.

I added five type of nuts to my diet, walnuts, almonds, Brazil nuts, pecans, and pistachios. I noticed a significant decrease in the number of times that I had to wake up urinate in only 3 day and more improvement by the tenth day. I now wake up overnight one to zero times to urinate. A huge improvement! I feel much more rested with better quality sleeping. In my sleep, I dream a lot more now, or I remember the dreams. I’d prefer not to dream so much. I eat two meals a day, no snacking. Eating close to the carnivore diet. Close to zero sugar, seed oils, and vegetable oil. No highly processed foods.

positive.text: Bone loss also has a significant impact on the appearance of aging skin, but if often completely overlooked. Interestingly, there was a study done of changes in facial bones that happened over time that showed the the biggest age-related aging change in the bone was a reduction in the height of the lower jaw bone and the overall shrinking of the lower jaw. Often when this happens, people can develop increased skin laxity and jowling and are recommended facelifts and other cosmetic intervention that don't address one of the root causes of the issue  Another study that supports the impact of bone health on aging was a study done in Asia that tested the aging of Asian women who were shown to have less skin laxity and signs of aging. The researchers hypothesized that this was due to an increased intake of vitamin K2 from natto, a food commonly eaten in Asian. Vitamin K2 helps the body better absorb and utilize calcium, decreasing age related bone loss, thereby reducing laxity caused by bone loss

positive.author: @Gringabeanpole
positive.text:
Lift with Cee is my go to. I’m a 25 year Pilates Instructor and once I retired at 60, I wanted a new challenge without giving up my Pilates routine. I had several people say, why would you change workouts, you’re in great shape.
But, I now feel, after a year with Cee, is both Pilates and Lifting should be in everyone’s routine because they hit muscles in different ways.
Cee’s 3 workouts a week of just 30 minutes fit nicely in my week.
Best thing about Lift with Cee. She doesn’t jibber jabber. That makes me nuts when instructors do that.
It’s also very easy to follow her form. I never had a problem with feeling like I was doing it wrong and may injure myself. I don’t think she’s targeted to beginners though. You probably should have lifted weights at least some or have been in the workout world.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @colettesimms9706
positive.text:
I am a “Workout with Cee aka Cheryl Coulombe” ❤ long timer here. I’ve worked out with Cee for 3 years and I’m turning 69 tomorrow!!! I’m stronger, in the best shape of my life, and still constantly challenged every day. Her information and coach training is spot on and she emphasizes dialing in your nutrition for fat loss and muscle building. This is very important to me since I have Osteopenia and am actively trying to improve my bone density naturally.

I really liked your assessment of other trainers but feel it’s also important to rate people that support both, a well rounded workout AND nutrition.🤩🌟💖

positive.author: @scottrobinson4611
positive.text:
I started exercising regularly 2 years ago, as an obese and sedentary 26M. I had started seeing some negative health effects like depression, sleep apnea, high blood pressure, resting HR of 75, and I even had two scares where I thought something was wrong with my heart (all was fine, thankfully). 

I started running to try to help myself. It was really hard to begin with, but I stuck with it and after a couple of months it became less shocking to my system and I started building some base fitness. 

Fast-forward 2 years, I'm in the greatest shape of my life. I'm down 20kg (45lbs). 
I feel healthy and strong. I run marathons for fun (??? this still feels weird), I go to the gym regularly, my body is starting to look lean and muscular in places (especially legs, thanks to running). 

I just feel like I have so many more options thanks to being fit. I can still sit on the couch all day, and eat until I feel sick, but I can also run 20 miles at a moment's notice without an issue. I can climb a mountain and feel good doing it.  
Perhaps more importantly, I just feel better in my head. My mood is better and more stable. Even when I am feeling down, I can do some exercise and it helps me feel better. 

My depression is gone. My sleep apnea is gone. My blood pressure is back to normal. My resting HR is now 48. 

It has taken a lot of effort, a lot of sweat and a shifting of my priorities to become an active person - my only regret is not starting 10 years earlier.

all.author: @scottrobinson4611
all.text:
I started exercising regularly 2 years ago, as an obese and sedentary 26M. I had started seeing some negative health effects like depression, sleep apnea, high blood pressure, resting HR of 75, and I even had two scares where I thought something was wrong with my heart (all was fine, thankfully). 

I started running to try to help myself. It was really hard to begin with, but I stuck with it and after a couple of months it became less shocking to my system and I started building some base fitness. 

Fast-forward 2 years, I'm in the greatest shape of my life. I'm down 20kg (45lbs). 
I feel healthy and strong. I run marathons for fun (??? this still feels weird), I go to the gym regularly, my body is starting to look lean and muscular in places (especially legs, thanks to running). 

I just feel like I have so many more options thanks to being fit. I can still sit on the couch all day, and eat until I feel sick, but I can also run 20 miles at a moment's notice without an issue. I can climb a mountain and feel good doing it.  
Perhaps more importantly, I just feel better in my head. My mood is better and more stable. Even when I am feeling down, I can do some exercise and it helps me feel better. 

My depression is gone. My sleep apnea is gone. My blood pressure is back to normal. My resting HR is now 48. 

It has taken a lot of effort, a lot of sweat and a shifting of my priorities to become an active person - my only regret is not starting 10 years earlier.

positive.author: @benblakeney7418
positive.text:
Since I didn't see sources for Serine mentioned other than as a supplement. A quick Google search - Serine sources include protein-rich foods like meat, fish, eggs, dairy, and soy, as well as nuts, legumes (chickpeas, lentils), and grains, but your body also produces it from glucose, glycine, and other metabolites. It's a nonessential amino acid, meaning your body can make it, but dietary intake is still important for brain health and function, especially from foods like soybeans, peanuts, almonds, sweet potatoes, and whey. 
So it would seem to be hard to be deficient in Serine to me, but I'm just a guy watching the video and not a health professional.

positive.author: @Bill-y1j
positive.text: I was dianosed with heart failure in 2024.  I was overweight and in poor health and left the hospital with a handful of meds (12 pills) that I was told I would have to take everyday for the rest of my life.  I made some immediate and severe lifestyle changes.  Completely overhauled my eating habbits and started walking 3 miles per day.  In just the first 7 months, lost 85lbs and normalized all my lab work.  I am now a 1/2 dose of 1 med and my heart condition has actually improved a little.  Still walking 3 miles per day and feeling better than ever :-)

positive.text:
Yes, recent research suggests grounding/earthing significantly affects mitochondria, improving their function by delivering antioxidant electrons from the Earth, which reduces harmful Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS), boosts ATP (energy) production (by 5-11%), and stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane potential, essentially reducing oxidative stress and supporting cellular energy. This helps protect mitochondria from damage, potentially enhancing cellular health and combating chronic inflammation linked to aging. 
Key Effects on Mitochondria
Reduced ROS: Grounding delivers electrons that neutralize free radicals, decreasing oxidative stress (ROS production by 22-33%) within mitochondria.
Increased ATP: Mitochondria under grounded conditions produce more ATP (energy) (5-11% increase).
Stabilized Membrane Potential: Grounding decreases the mitochondrial membrane potential (by 5-6%), indicating improved bioenergetics and stability.
Antioxidant Protection: The Earth's free electrons act as antioxidants, protecting the mitochondrial matrix and DNA from oxidative damage. 
How it Works (The Theory)
Electron Transfer: The body acts as a conductor, receiving free electrons from the Earth.
Neutralizing Free Radicals: These electrons neutralize inflammatory free radicals, reducing the body's electrical tension and oxidative burden.
Restoring Natural State: Grounding helps restore the body's natural electrical potential, promoting a calmer internal environment crucial for optimal mitochondrial function, as chronic disconnection from the Earth can disrupt this balance. 
Implications for Health
By improving mitochondrial function, grounding may help combat chronic inflammation and support overall health, with implications for longevity, cardiovascular health, and recovery from stress-related conditions.

transcript.summary: The speaker discusses a Japanese night routine that helps reduce cortisol and improve sleep by incorporating practices such as dimming lights, taking a hot bath, and practicing gratitude.

positive.author: @DenshaOtoko2
positive.text: I tried this starting in 2005 after a Japan trip. Slept like a baby.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @jeffrey322
positive.text:
The 7 Practices:

Stop Eating 2-3 Hours Before Bed: Digestion keeps your core temperature elevated and cortisol high. Early dinner (6-7 PM) allows your body to finish processing food, drop temperature, and signal your brain it's time to sleep.

Take a Hot Bath (The Ofuro): Not because it relaxes you—but because when you get out, your core temperature drops rapidly. That temperature drop triggers melatonin release. Get out 60-90 minutes before bed for peak effect.

Dim the Lights: Your brain uses light to decide what time it is. Bright lights = cortisol stays high, melatonin delayed. Dim lights 2 hours before bed = melatonin rises naturally, cortisol drops, sleep mode activates.

The Digital Sunset: No screens 60 minutes before bed. Netflix isn't winding down—it's stimulation. Every cliffhanger, notification, and scroll keeps your nervous system in stress mode. Screen-free evenings reset your circadian rhythm.

The Yoru no Sanpo (Evening Walk): A 10-20 minute gentle walk after dinner helps digestion and naturally lowers cortisol. Not exercise—just gentle movement, cool air, and transition from day to night.

Reading Time (Yomu Jikan): Physical books only. Reading transfers your focus from your own anxious thoughts to someone else's world. 6 minutes of reading reduces stress by 68%—more than music, walking, or tea.

Gratitude Practice (Kansha): Before bed, reflect on three small things that went well. Gratitude activates your parasympathetic nervous system, releases oxytocin and serotonin, and drops cortisol. Not forced positivity—just shifting attention from problems to gifts.

Why This Works:

Every practice targets a different type of cortisol. You're not forcing sleep—you're removing what blocks it.

Early dinner = drops digestive cortisol
Hot bath = drops thermal cortisol
Dim lights = drops visual cortisol
Digital sunset = drops stimulation cortisol
Evening walk = drops physical cortisol
Reading = drops mental cortisol
Gratitude = drops emotional cortisol

Sleep isn't something you do. It's something you allow. When cortisol drops, sleep comes naturally. Every time.

The Bottom Line:

You don't have bad sleep because something is wrong with you. You have bad sleep because your evenings are designed to keep you awake.

Bright lights. Stimulating screens. Late meals. No transition. No stillness.

But when you give your body the signals it needs, everything changes.

You don't need all seven practices at once. Pick one. Start tonight. Let it become part of your rhythm.

Because sleep isn't a reward for being tired enough. It's a result of being safe enough.

And when your body feels safe, it rests deeply.

###

all.author: @jeffrey322
all.text:
The 7 Practices:

Stop Eating 2-3 Hours Before Bed: Digestion keeps your core temperature elevated and cortisol high. Early dinner (6-7 PM) allows your body to finish processing food, drop temperature, and signal your brain it's time to sleep.

Take a Hot Bath (The Ofuro): Not because it relaxes you—but because when you get out, your core temperature drops rapidly. That temperature drop triggers melatonin release. Get out 60-90 minutes before bed for peak effect.

Dim the Lights: Your brain uses light to decide what time it is. Bright lights = cortisol stays high, melatonin delayed. Dim lights 2 hours before bed = melatonin rises naturally, cortisol drops, sleep mode activates.

The Digital Sunset: No screens 60 minutes before bed. Netflix isn't winding down—it's stimulation. Every cliffhanger, notification, and scroll keeps your nervous system in stress mode. Screen-free evenings reset your circadian rhythm.

The Yoru no Sanpo (Evening Walk): A 10-20 minute gentle walk after dinner helps digestion and naturally lowers cortisol. Not exercise—just gentle movement, cool air, and transition from day to night.

Reading Time (Yomu Jikan): Physical books only. Reading transfers your focus from your own anxious thoughts to someone else's world. 6 minutes of reading reduces stress by 68%—more than music, walking, or tea.

Gratitude Practice (Kansha): Before bed, reflect on three small things that went well. Gratitude activates your parasympathetic nervous system, releases oxytocin and serotonin, and drops cortisol. Not forced positivity—just shifting attention from problems to gifts.

Why This Works:

Every practice targets a different type of cortisol. You're not forcing sleep—you're removing what blocks it.

Early dinner = drops digestive cortisol
Hot bath = drops thermal cortisol
Dim lights = drops visual cortisol
Digital sunset = drops stimulation cortisol
Evening walk = drops physical cortisol
Reading = drops mental cortisol
Gratitude = drops emotional cortisol

Sleep isn't something you do. It's something you allow. When cortisol drops, sleep comes naturally. Every time.

The Bottom Line:

You don't have bad sleep because something is wrong with you. You have bad sleep because your evenings are designed to keep you awake.

Bright lights. Stimulating screens. Late meals. No transition. No stillness.

But when you give your body the signals it needs, everything changes.

You don't need all seven practices at once. Pick one. Start tonight. Let it become part of your rhythm.

Because sleep isn't a reward for being tired enough. It's a result of being safe enough.

And when your body feels safe, it rests deeply.

###

positive.author: @spitalhelles3380
positive.text: The most important nootropics are sleep and exercise

positive.author: @_Keith_
positive.text:
Creatine (0:00-0:52): Acts as a backup battery for quick brain energy, supporting focus, memory, and clear thinking. It's especially beneficial for those who consume less meat, as meat is a primary source. Creatine monohydrate is the most effective form.

Omega-3 Fatty Acids (0:55-1:56): These fats, particularly DHA and EPA, keep brain cells flexible for smooth signal transmission and help control inflammation, promoting calmness and balanced mood. Low levels can lead to poor focus, mood swings, and impaired learning and memory. Found in fatty fish, they must be obtained through diet or supplements.

Alpha GPC (1:59-2:50): A fast-acting form of choline that helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical crucial for focus and quick thinking. It can improve clarity and recall, especially when intense focus is needed. While choline is in some foods, most people fall short.

Citicoline (2:52-3:47): Another choline-based compound that boosts acetylcholine and helps build healthy cell membranes. It can improve mental clarity and recall, particularly for multitasking and learning new things. Citicoline is not found in food and must be supplemented.

Curcumin (3:49-4:21): The active compound in turmeric that reduces inflammation and oxidative stress in the brain. It also boosts BDNF, which strengthens brain connections, leading to clearer thinking, better mood, and improved focus. Supplements often include black pepper extract for better absorption.

Magnesium L-Threonate (4:23-5:23): This is the only form of magnesium that effectively crosses into the brain, helping to calm overactive pathways, strengthen neuronal connections, and support long-term memory. It can alleviate poor sleep, racing thoughts, and difficulty concentrating. While found in some foods, most people don't get enough from diet alone.

Bacopa Monnieri (5:26-6:12): Helps improve memory by reducing oxidative stress and supporting serotonin and dopamine. It strengthens neural connections, making learning smoother and enhancing recall and concentration. Its beneficial compounds are primarily found in supplements.

L-Theanine (6:14-7:13): Promotes calm alertness, especially when paired with caffeine. It boosts alpha brain waves, leading to clean focus, longer attention, and fewer jitters than caffeine alone. It's found in green tea, but supplementing provides sufficient amounts to balance caffeine's effects.

Phosphatidylserine (7:16-8:02): A fatty compound that keeps brain cells flexible and responsive, ensuring fast and accurate signal transmission. It aids in smooth task switching, information processing, and managing the stress hormone cortisol. Small amounts are found in foods, but supplements provide the form the brain absorbs best.

Ginkgo Biloba (8:04-8:42): Boosts blood flow to the brain, delivering more oxygen and nutrients to areas responsible for memory, focus, and quick thinking. It also acts as an antioxidant, protecting neurons. The useful compounds come from leaf extract, typically consumed as a supplement.

negative.author: @r-l-h7p
negative.text: I suggest everyone actually looks up and reads the studies based on which many of these "brain-boosting" claims are based on. For instance, one of the most-cited trials on the effect of creatine on the brain by Rae et al., 2003 was in vegetarians who may start with lower creatine, and even then it’s mainly working-memory test scores and not “IQ went up and life changed.” Other meta-analyses generally find small average effects on memory and often no clear improvement in overall cognition. Having proper sleep etiquette and quality, meditating for 15-20 mins a day, and not eating processed (junk) food will already do wonders for the majority of people suffering from a mushy brain..

positive.text: Los Angeles, CA @ 9 am. I started listening to this extraordinary video not because I needed to fall asleep but because I’ve been interested in human evolution, in this case anthropology, since my teens. What piqued my  interest was a college course in anthropology where I learned there were two branches in anthropology: physical and cultural. Around that time (late 1960s) there was a question of whether humans evolved from ancestral primates that were naturally non aggressive peaceful vegetarians or aggressive predators that hunted animals for food and fought for territorial imperative. What I like about this video was that it provided an explanation of the impact of physical and cultural aspects that created today’s humans. I didn’t realized that human didn’t change much since 50,000 years ago. If this subject matter interests you, look for YouTube videos that track the migration of modern day humans out of Africa about 100,000 years ago from a population known today as the “click” people. 👍❤

positive.text: Keeping the fat off from a physical what to do is easy. It’s the mental part that typically makes it so hard. Nov last year I was 205lbs (5'5" Male) started off by just tracking calories, getting steps (15K a day) and some light weights from some 15lb dumbbells and a 40lb ez bar I had given to me, on July 1 this year I joined the gym for the first time and have been going 4 days a week with a real training plan, haven't missed a session since.

Today I am 138.6lbs my original goal was to get to 135lb which still might be accurate I can see my up abs when flexing but I also have some fat around the bottom abs

this last few points is 100000% the hardest part of this journey, I have noticed the closer I eat to maintenance does help keep the scale moving, its only when I try to create a big deficit it stops, probably due my NEAT and other activities are less the bigger the deficit thats when I notice the plateau.

this video was great

positive.author: @erikacomfort3343
positive.text: This video is literally so helpful for me right now. I’ve been experiencing consistent health anxiety for ten months following what we think was a bad viral reaction. The fact that I’m still not back to normal ten months after being sick leads my anxiety to think the doctors missed something or that there’s something deeper and harder to detect going on (even though all of my symptoms still reasonably align with post viral illnesses). My anxiety will take over when my symptoms get worse, or even if something triggers it randomly, and my brain will mistake that for intuition and think ‘I just know I’m dying, I can just feel it.’ Then I urgently want every medical test ever made. But if I give it a day or two, or even a few hours sometimes, I will return mostly back to normal once I calm down, especially if my symptoms subside again. This has been hell and this video(in addition to the health anxiety video) are lifesavers. It’s just my anxiety. It’s not my intuition.
positive.label: Positive

Menopause supplements are everywhere right now, and many of them are marketed specifically for skin health. Some of these products do have emerging evidence behind them, but the benefits tend to be modest and the marketing often exaggerates what they can realistically do.

Thanks again for being here!

positive.author: @hotsauce7124
positive.text:
1.  Blood pressure is regulated between 5 systems in the body: electrolytes, Hormones, nervous system, muscles, blood.
2.  Electrolytes include: sodium, potassium and magnesium.  If you struggle with proper potassium and magnesium levels then you will have a sodium imbalance; leading to high blood pressure.
3. Salt raises blood pressure, salt actually changes the way your cells respond to insulin and salt distorts your thirst.
4. Don't eat fast foods, bread, restaurant food; they are high in sodium.
5. Reduce saturated fat intake: Animal fat, dairy, coconut oil, vegetable oil, seed oil.
6. A DASH diet can help lower blood pressure.
7. A Whole food plant based diet can help lower blood pressure.
8. A Mediterranean diet can help lower blood pressure.
9. A Nordic diet can help lower blood pressure.
10. A low sodium/high potassium diet can help lower blood pressure.
11. In the short term, all these diets can lower your mercury levels: 7mm per Hg 
12. Be wary of diets that promote water loss without correcting potassium and magnesium like a low carbohydrate,diets that promote calorie restriction and ketogenic diets.
13. Best way to lower your blood pressure is to move your big muscle groups for 10-15 minutes per day: walking, cycling, and squatting.  Check with a medical doctor before starting any exercise or diet.
14.  Get yourself insulin sensitive.
15. Check your blood pressure.  If your blood pressure is naturally low then check with a doctor before adopting a diet.  You do not want your blood pressure getting too low or bottoming out.
16. Eat foods rich in  potassium and magnesium: leafy greens and beans.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text: Was prescribed to take magnesium for four years after having major cancer surgery.   Starting after surgery I had chronic fatigue and Everytime I tried to walk, even using a walker, I would get weak, dizzy, and light headed to the point of having to sit down immediately or else put my head down on a counter top. positive.author: @Cody_Trading
positive.text:
Just lost 30lbs in 3 months (12 weeks) - 227 -> 197lbs. I ate 2000 cals everyday, about 175g protein, 65g fat, rest carbs. On Sundays I started adding in some more cals as a refeed in the form of a 70% cocoa chocolate bar and a large strawberry blizzard from DQ.

I worked out 3 days a week, Mon, Wed, Fri Push, Legs, Pull. On workout days I would walk 13 to 15k steps and on non workout days I would walk 20k steps. My incline bench press has remained the same so not sure if I am losing any muscle. I just had a burning desire to get under 200lbs.

Next goal is 190lbs and then 185lbs and then I will hit maintenance for a bit. I want to get a 6 pack for summer. I ate the same meal pretty much everyday, this makes things easier. Be consistent with your diet, workout, get a good amount of steps, and stop drinking for awhile, I didn't drink once in the 3 months.

positive.author: @shazzy7311
positive.text:
I’ve been struggling with perimenopause which caused my nervous system to be hyper-sensitive. Cortisol raging!  I had tried to CUT sugar and realized all it did was make my liver dump mounds of it in my system because it was listening to my cortisol.  My first step is calming my body and allowing sugars back in, but I’m doing that through small amounts of honey in the morning and my new favourite mid morning snack at work is a date with real peanut butter!! SO GOOD!! 
I’ve been gaining weight the past 3 months, but I’m allowing it to be part of the strategy since I think my body is settling and now swinging into protective mode.  I’m starting super light weights because even a bit of exercise seems to absolutely exhaust my muscles.  And I have tried very slight rebounding after breakfast (like 50 small easy jumps).  
I’m trying not to freak out about the weight and to love my body for being protective… but also desperately want to get back to where I feel like I have a better rhythm.
Thank you for your grounded solid channel. I look forward to more. This has been a hard but enlightening three years for me!

I started intermittent fasting at the beginning of the year and I’m now in my 4th week. I also started paying attention to hydration using a simple formula: body weight in pounds ÷ 2 = ounces of water per day. Then I divide that by the size of my water glass to track how many glasses I need.

I’ve also learned that both dehydration and drinking too much water can be dangerous. As my weight changes, I plan to adjust my hydration accordingly.

positive.author: @freon_bale
positive.text: There is another option. Hibernate mode, which all Windows machines are capable of. It works like Sleep Mode, except that instead of keeping RAM powered, and everything else off, it copies everything in RAM to the hard drive, and then turns everything off. You can leave a computer in Hibernate literally forever, and it will not deplete the battery at all. The downside? When it turns back on, it must copy everything from the hard drive back into RAM, which may take a second or two. With today's modern NVMe drives, it's barely noticeable. Does it hurt your computer? No, that's ridiculous. Does it cause your system to be less stable if used over and over, debatable. I would reboot a Windows PC at least once every 3-4 weeks. With heavy use, that's about Windows' limit in terms of performance degradation, though it would still be stable.

neutral.text:
Just to clarify:
A restart is not the same as a shutdown and start. Here are the key differences and steps to understand their behavior:

Restart

Closes all programs and processes, including the Windows kernel (core of the operating system).

Performs a cold boot, ensuring a clean start for the system.

Recommended for: Installing updates or software. Resolving system errors or driver issues. Applying group policies.

Shutdown and Start

With Fast Startup enabled (default in Windows 8, 10, and 11), shutdown saves the Windows kernel to disk (a hybrid hibernation state).

On starting, the kernel is reloaded, making the boot process faster but not fully resetting the system.

Recommended for: Turning off the computer for extended periods. Saving power when not in use.

all.text: Dr. Vonda, I’ve been following you for quite some time and I love your messaging! The only issue I have with this message today is the design problem? I differ in opinion. positive.author: @WATTYATHINK
positive.text: Commented before, but will again - just to show some support for your commonsense post. I'm nearly 78 now and approaching 3 years after having a hip replacement. I'm 5'8", and I weighed nearly 260lbs at the time of my operation.  I started to watch my diet, and started walking shortly before my operation and dove into it seriously after the operation. I now weigh (this morning 170lbs), and I do at least 2 hrs on the treadmill every morning. My diet was simply to cut down on my meals and walking.  Recently, I've started to do some dumbbell work and those stretching routines (tai chi). My wife of 52 years is also walking with me, and we are averaging over 25,000 steps daily. Our one vice is walking to McD's every night for a muffin and coffee (about 1 hr walk). As you have suggested, I eat everything but have cut down on the portions, I avoid adding salt to my food, and I cut out sweets. I don't count calories, but I normally cut at least one meal a couple of times a week and drink a meal replacement drink instead.

positive.author: @DrAlexWibberley
positive.text:
Hello everyone and thank you for watching! I really hope you found this video useful. I read all of your comments and try to reply to as many as I can every day across the channel. The community on this channel is absolutely fantastic.... people sharing their stories, supporting each other, and learning together. It's amazing to see. 

It means a lot to me that this has become a space where people are interested in the simple things that keep us healthy and prevent problems before they ever reach the hospital. If there’s a topic you’d like me to explain in a future video, please let me know in the comments.

If you’d like to support me, the best thing you can do is click the like button and subscribe. It really helps these videos reach more people who might benefit from them, and it allows me to keep making them! 

My goal with these videos is simple: to help as many people as possible stay healthier and avoid ending up in the emergency department if we can. 

Wishing you all the best, and thanks again!

Dr Alex 😊

negative.author: @liamjeffery4565
negative.text:
Good episode overall. You did well pressing Gardner on the protein recommendations, but I wish you had corrected or asked for more clarification from Ty throughout this. It felt like a few statements that misalign with the broader consensus on US public health slid by a bit too easily.

Ty brought up some great nuance that people actually need to enjoy the food they eat for a diet to be sustainable, and that incorporating some animal foods can be better than the ultra-processed junk a lot of people might eat instead. It's also fair to point out that nutrient deficiencies are an issue for certain demographics even in the US.

But he kept bringing up global data on severe undernutrition to justify higher animal product intake. That sometimes makes sense globally, but when you're talking about US guidelines where the main public health crises are calorie overconsumption, cardiovascular disease, and a massive lack of fiber it really muddies the waters. Optimizing a diet for a malnourished population is just fundamentally different than optimizing for the average American.

The talk around saturated fat and full-fat dairy too. Glossing over the established link between the saturated fat in full-fat dairy and increased ApoB leaves people with a dangerously simplified takeaway. It's frustrating to hear him use an n=1 personal anecdote about swapping eggs for oatmeal to cast doubt on the massive body of evidence showing the cardiovascular benefits of whole grains over foods high in saturated fat and cholesterol.

Also, giving that much grace to the anti-seed oil narrative without anchoring it back to the reality that replacing saturated fats with polyunsaturated fats consistently improves outcomes felt like a missed opportunity.

Same goes for the protein discussion. Pushing more protein for satiety and weight loss sounds great in clinical theory, but human behavior is messy. In practice, telling the general US population to eat more protein usually just translates to them eating more high-saturated-fat meats, rather than the fiber-rich plant proteins the population actually needs.

positive.text:
I'm 70 years old. After bitterly complaining about dizziness and fatigue, my doctor took me off blood pressure medications.

positive.text:
💯  thank you, Dr. Corbin  😊 ❤  here's the TLDR:

This video features Dr. Karen Corbin, a PhD researcher, who discusses the gut microbiome and its critical role in metabolism, mood, and longevity. The conversation highlights how the gut is a "metabolism show" (1:46) with trillions of microbial species that actively metabolize undigested food, sending signals and hormones throughout the body.

Key takeaways from the discussion include:
The importance of fiber: Fiber is the preferred food for beneficial gut microorganisms (10:09). When these microbes are starved by consuming ultra-processed foods, they can become "hangry" (11:38) and produce inflammatory molecules (11:41), potentially leading to a "leaky gut" (12:28).
The gut-brain connection: Microbes communicate with the brain through pathways like the vagus nerve (7:37) and can even produce neurotransmitters (7:46), influencing overall well-being.
Diet can remodel your gut: Dr. Corbin shares research showing that specific dietary changes can remodel the gut microbiome, leading to a reduction in absorbed calories (0:06) and an increase in satiety hormones (13:17).
Four research-backed levers for gut health:
    1.  Dietary fiber: Found in vegetables, fruits, and whole grains (29:26).
    2.  Resistant starch: Present in foods like beans, quinoa, pharaoh, oats, and green bananas. Its content increases when starches are cooled after cooking (30:32).
    3.  Whole foods: These have larger pieces that reach the colon for microbial digestion and are less processed (30:49).
    4.  Avoiding ultra-processed foods: These are mechanically and chemically altered, which is not beneficial for the microbiome (31:12).
No standardized microbiome test: As of now, there isn't a reliable diagnostic test to confidently assess gut microbiome health or prescribe specific probiotics (22:58). Dr. Corbin advises against spending large amounts on expensive probiotics due to the current lack of scientific evidence (23:38).

The video emphasizes adopting an "abundance mindset" (38:05) by focusing on incorporating beneficial foods rather than restricting intake, highlighting that a well-fed gut microbiome can benefit various health profiles and lifestyle choices.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text:
I agree with his cautions about Metformin and PPIs, but I was disappointed that he didn’t explain how to actually reverse diabetic neuropathy. After looking into published medical journal studies on Alpha Lipoic Acid and Benfotiamine, I decided to try it myself — 600mg of ALA and 450mg of Benfotiamine each evening. I began noticing improvement after about 30 days, and by the 3-month mark, my neuropathy was completely gone.

It’s frustrating that more doctors aren’t aware of this. Even my own doctor didn’t believe me until I printed out one of the studies and showed it to him. (For context, I was already taking methylcobalamin and a full B-complex vitamin with methylfolate.)

positive.author: @kubraaydilek5667
positive.text: Important conversation about transparency and systemic barriers in healthcare. Prior authorization and administrative processes often affect patients in ways they don’t fully see until it becomes a challenge. Raising awareness about these structural issues is essential for meaningful reform.

positive.text: The point about data transparency was important. Without clear reporting on denial rates and turnaround times, it’s hard to hold anyone accountable. Metrics matter here. 📊

negative.author: @SerenOzturk-g5x
negative.text: From a patient’s perspective, prior authorization is basically invisible until the moment it suddenly becomes a roadblock. Most people don’t even know what it is until they’re told they can’t get a medication, test, or procedure they urgently need. And by the time they learn the term, they’re already stuck dealing with delays, paperwork, and confusing back-and-forth calls. That kind of disconnect makes the whole system feel untrustworthy and exhausting. It’s no surprise it creates so much frustration, because patients are left feeling like they’re being punished for rules they were never even told existed.

positive.author: @amandamittleman84
positive.text:
As a personal trainer with 30+ years of experience and a Master's thesis focused on exercise intensity and body composition across a lifetime — including DEXA measurements on 100+ postmenopausal women ranging from elite athletes to sedentary controls — I have enormous respect for research. AND I'll say what the data alone can't:
Reading studies is one part of exercise prescription. Working with real women — in real bodies, real hormones, real lives — is another.
If data were enough, we wouldn't have 82% of Americans metabolically unhealthy with more information available than ever before.
Women are not small men. Some of us can train with high intensity and recover well. Many cannot — especially in perimenopause and menopause, when hormonal shifts fundamentally change how we respond to stress, recover from training, and lose or gain body composition.
I say this with love and respect for the science: you cannot fully understand the nuances of perimenopause until you live it. I couldn't. And I had the data, the degree, and 20+ years of experience when I hit it.
One size does not fit all. The best exercise prescription meets the woman in front of you — not just the study population.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @MathStatsMe
positive.text: Even with daily yoga a few years ago, as I started into perimenopause, I started getting all kinds of tendonitis issues, which require a broad range of tactics to manage, including massage, PT, and strength training. I'm kicking proverbial butt now in comparison to before gaining more muscle through strength training than yoga alone could provide. I still love the yoga, but appreciate having a broader range of targeted strength training approaches. I have a disabled son who relies on me to be physically robust, so this is a big deal to me.
positive.label: Positive

A few notes/highlights. I realize this is a highly controversial historic study and many may have pre-formed opinions. If you are similar with the study in question, keep in mind wouldn’t cover it if I didn’t feel I had an original take. I do address the common criticisms of the study, including attrition, trans fats and more. And, as always, for those who want the written breakdown and all the references, see StayCurious Metabolism letter, here: https://staycuriousmetabolism.substack.com/p/lowering-cholesterol-killed-a-study?r=40ekz2 

I also realize there was a recent, and rather controversial “seed oil debate” (not really a debate) on the Drive with Peter Attia with guest Layne Norton. To get ahead of the question, since it’s been coming up like a game of whack-a-mole this past week, the opponent who pulled out was Paul Saladino who offered me in his place. Unfortunately, Layne strongly opposed citing a false rumor he started. 
Evidence trail:  https://x.com/nicknorwitz/status/2013373495590134025?s=20 

Frankly, I feel the debate was mis-managed. 
Thoughts here: https://x.com/nicknorwitz/status/2014350441178419329?s=20 

WARNING, if you want to avoid drama, don’t click on the above links and save yourself some cortisol.
And…
My Debate with Paul Saladino on Seed oils: https://youtu.be/EsrXMhCg6Dk?si=2Kcp8CKT2Ovu2aRz

negative.text: Chris Ramsden, the researcher who unearthed the MCE data, also unearthed data from the Sydney Heart Study. The SHS was performed as a secondary prevention study whereas the MCE was for primary prevention. The SHS (performed at the same time as the MCE) showed the same results. Swapping out SatFat for Omega 6 PUFAs was detrimental. And, the SHS results were, similarly, buried in the same way. This has all the hallmarks of Keys' influence in this area. Hiding one study can be a conspiracy theory, but hiding 2 that disprove your beliefs is a pattern.

positive.author: @LoevensRambles
positive.text: After losing 36 kgs my biology started working against me. I have been worse at eating healthy and craved more snacks and unhealthy foods. The number on the scales didn't move, and I was constantly cold and tired and unknowingly I had become less active. I decided to take a break from the stress of having to think about what I ate all the time, but still making sure to get my protein. But the big win for me on Wegovy is, that when I don't think of what I eat and just live my life, I don't gain weight anymore, that was unheard of before. So I decided to count that as a victory in itself. The scale didn't move for at least 4 months. I started feeling less tired, less inactive and like my body finally realized that it wasn't starving.  I became ready and motivated to give weightloss another go. So I went back to eating healthier foods and cutting down on snacks etc. And the weight started coming off almost immediately. I feel like I need to be on Wegovy for the rest of my life, because if it wasnt for Wegovy, I could easily had put those 36 kgs back on in those 4 months. Instead the weight stood still and now it's going down again. It's nice to know that I can be gentle with myself and give myself breaks every now and then, without gaining any weight. I now count  not gaining weight, as just as big of a victory as the weightloss. I am about half the way to my goal weight, and it may take longer than I first thought but I know I will get there.
positive.label: Positive

It’s easy to get to hung up on the “losing weight” vs actually just maintaining what is already lost.

positive.author: @yu8mophoo329
positive.text:
Dr. Robert Harrison explains that vision loss in older adults is increasing, often due to damage occurring overnight when the retina doesn't receive enough oxygen and nutrients (0:56). He emphasizes that this isn't solely due to age, but rather to preventable damage (0:31).

The video highlights seven fruits that can naturally support eye health and repair overnight, along with five crucial rules for consuming them to maximize their benefits.

Key Fruits for Eye Health:

Kiwi (3:53): Rich in lutein, zeaxanthin, and vitamin C, it protects the retina from oxidative stress and reduces cataract formation. Golden kiwi is preferred for its higher lutein content and lower acidity (5:10).
Watermelon (6:13): Its high water content supports tear film, while lycopene protects retinal cells. The white rind contains citrulline, which boosts nitric oxide for better blood flow to the retina (6:59).
Black Currants (8:25): Exceptionally rich in anthocyanins, they reduce inflammation in retinal blood vessels and support night vision by regenerating rhodopsin. Standardized extract is recommended due to limited fresh availability (9:15).
Blueberries (10:49): High in anthocyanins, they protect photoreceptors from oxidative damage and reduce the risk of macular degeneration. Wild blueberries are preferred for their higher antioxidant content, and they should not be consumed with dairy (11:33).

positive.author: @roblloyd1879
positive.text: Had severe arthritis in my right hand for many years to the point were my doctor was considering steroid injections. I have also had back pain from a road accident when I was 16. Had followed the government and NHS guidelines on diet for many years, cut out animal fats, used vegetable and seed oils, margarine and limited eggs and dairy. Red meats were very rare in my diet. After my wife passed away 5 years ago I decided to change my diet completely. Eliminated veg and seed oils, started eating lots of eggs, cheese, butter and dairy. Red meat and fish often, particularly pork as it is a major source of essential nutrients. Cook mainly in animal fats. Cut down on carbs but still plenty of fruit and vegetables. Use olive oil and occasionally 'Cold Pressed' rapeseed oil. I cook from fresh or frozen with ready meals a rarity. Mainly a pizza once every couple of months as a treat. Within a year my arthritis had gone, I lost over 2 stone and I have just realised my back pain has gone. Not bad for an old codger aged 78. I can still chase the youngest grandchildren round and play garden badminton with them. My conclusion is 90% of good health is diet!!!! Always had backache from the age of 16 when I decided to argue with a van, the van won and I had a broken leg, a back injury and some short term memory brain damage. Over time the brain learns to ignore the pain although it is always present. Suddenly realised my back pain has gone. Says it all really. A real food diet is king!
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @shizuokaBLUES
positive.text:
Central coastal Japan and its time to turn off my light.  Mid February and we are now in the quiet time of the year before the blossoms open in full, and the nights are still cold, clear and dry.   It feels like our lives and the stability most of us have enjoyed and thrived on are on a tight rope now. But so it goes through our eons on this planet.  
I’m afraid it’s our ego and our greed that is to blame for this. 
But for tonight, and hopefully tomorrow it’s warm and peaceful here and I’ll walk 90 minutes each way to work along the canal and take in the sunshine and bird sounds. Life is good on earth…. It’s just fleeting. 
Goodnight all,  look up at the stars and be thankful for your consciousness and forget our troubles.

neutral.text:
Great podcast, Gary Brecka. Dr. Shepherd was a great guest.

What stood out most is how clearly the connection was made between women’s health and the realities many don’t always name… access, equity and the lived experiences of Black and brown women within the medical system. When we talk about menopause, longevity and hormone health, we can’t separate the science from the systems people are navigating to receive care.

There was also a powerful throughline here: when we begin to center those with the least access to resources, the standard of care rises for everyone.
That’s how real change happens. And conversations like this don’t just inform… they expand who feels seen, who feels included, and who feels empowered to seek answers. This is how the narrative shifts. Midlife isn’t a pause. It’s a shift.

Dr. Hyman and Dr. Hinohara hit on a crucial point about systemic inflammation. Here's why synergy is key:
1. Chia's ALA needs conversion to active EPA/DHA, which is less efficient as we age.
2. Turmeric with black pepper significantly boosts curcumin absorption for anti-inflammatory effects.
3. Vitamin C-rich fruits enhance ALA conversion and provide vital antioxidants.
4. Probiotic foods combined with chia's prebiotics build a healthy gut, reducing inflammation at its source.
Consistency in these combinations truly unlocks chia's potential.

Dr. Hyman and Dr. Hino, this is the perfect biological explanation for a widespread health failure! As a Senior Health Specialist, I constantly encounter the 'Health Halo' [01:06] problem with chia seeds.

Turmeric + Black Pepper [06:54]: Piperine increases Curcumin absorption by 2000%.
Probiotics (Yogurt/Kefir) [13:08]: Restores gut flora to support the prebiotic fiber in chia.
Vitamin C (Berries/Kiwi) [10:42]: Enhances the conversion of ALA to active omega-3s.
Pro-Tip: Emphasize avoiding dry chia seeds [16:50] and flavored, sugary yogurt [17:16]—these habits actively negate the anti-inflammatory benefits. Essential, practical biochemistry! Subscribed!

Hello everyone and thank you for watching! I really hope you found this video useful. I read all of your comments and try to reply to as many as I can every day across the channel. If you’d like to support me, the best thing you can do is click the like button and subscribe. It really helps these videos reach more people who might benefit from them, and it allows me to keep making them!

Wishing you all the best, and thanks again!

Dr Alex 😊

positive.text: hearing you explain all the misconceptions around bariatric surgery really stood out to me, because so many people genuinely think it’s some quick fix when in reality it’s a whole journey. I liked the part about how minimally invasive techniques help people get home sooner, since honestly the hospital environment really does slow recovery for a lot of folks. and the point about obesity being connected to things like diabetes, sleep apnea, depression, even changes in puberty or menopause, shows how complex it really is. The way your team works together every day with dietitians, social workers, nurses and surgeons says a lot about why long term results matter more than just the surgery itself. I’m also curious about the future of the field, especially with medications and new techniques becoming a bigger part of the process. do you think the balance between surgery and meds will shift even more over the next few years?

positive.text:
Freeze Response/Depressed
1.  Get upright/more vertical. 
2.  Get morning light in the first hour (outdoors preferably).
3.  Get heat (gradual)/cold (faster).
4.  Vagus Nerve:  Hum or long sigh.  Massage your face.  
5.   Structure your morning: Exercise/Walk dog/Open blinds/Upbeat music.
6.  Positivity:  Gratitude, list 3 things.   Help someone. 
7.  Too busy:  Balance with a hike or a nap.  No tv/phone.
8.   Orange zest/peppermint.

all.text: I am 76 and was born in Indonesia of Indonesian, Chinese, and European extraction. I have used turmeric and ginger all my life. Suffering from arthritis since my 50's and taking lots of ibuprofen for years for pain, I finally learned to make my own version of "golden tea" learned from this website and others. Starting with a cup of heated water, I add turmeric powder, shaved fresh ginger, dried coconut milk powder, olive or flaxseed oil, and a pinch of ground pepper. Pain is but a memory now. Just a note: be sure to brush your teeth and rinse your mouth afterward to avoid staining teeth.

positive.text:
Great video!
I was having a consistent problem with the sensation of dirt in my throat after any moto. It was like I was gagging coughing and couldn’t clear my throat, a burning feeling, couldn’t even speak for several minutes. I used to believe it was only from having my mouth open to breathe, dust inhalation, so I concentrated on 100% nose breathing. That was helpful, but the problem still persisted. My doctor suggested it was induced gastrointestinal gerd from woops and jumping. Stomach contents were going up and burning my throat! 
So as long as I don’t eat anything or overdo the sports drinks 2 hrs or so before racing I’m fine. Plenty of plain water is fine. Problem solved in my case.

Summary (Very Short & Punchy)
- New research (2025 human study) shows Taxifolin (Dehydroquercetin) can improve metabolism safely.
- Results: 300 mg/day for 6 months → modest weight loss (+ better HDL) with zero side effects.
How it works:
- Activates brown fat (UCP1, PGC1α, PRDM16) → more calorie burn
- Boosts FGF-21 → AMPK activation, better insulin sensitivity
- Helps muscles absorb glucose even without insulin
- Strong anti-inflammatory & antioxidant effect (NRF2 ↑, NF-κB ↓)
- Why it matters: burns cleaner, stores less, and protects metabolism from inflammation.
- Best combos: cold exposure, berberine, omega-3s.
- Not a magic pill—works best with fasting, exercise, sleep, and good nutrition.

neutral.author: @twowheelsintokyo7039
neutral.text: The important thing is motivation. Losing weight while cycling is a combination of diet and exercise. If you have the motivation to get out on your bike each day, you will have more motivation to regulate your diet. I used to ride in fast groups, and spent a year racing, and these were a blast. Now I'm older, not so fast, and not so motivated to compete. But I love cycling, A good ride gives me a good workout, and it gets the endorphins flowing. Exercise regularly, your body starts getting hooked on these endorphins (secreted by your body to deal with the physical stress and pain). Pretty soon you don't have to force yourself to go out and ride, you can't help yourself, your body wants to do it. At this point it is easier to eat better. Beyond a certain level, like if you are riding 2 more more hours per day, weight loss is inevitable no matter how much you eat. But as most of us don't have that much time to spend in the saddle, changing one's diet helps. For myself, reducing or eliminating sugar, bread, rice, and such makes a huge difference, and the weight falls off.

My goal with these videos is simple: to help as many people as possible stay healthier and avoid ending up in the emergency department if we can. 

Wishing you all the best, and thanks again!

Dr Alex 😊

I became obese and pre-diabetic with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. My doctor gave me three choices: gastric surgery, GLP-1 injections or dietary & lifestyle changes. These changes would also be required for the surgical approach and the injections. I opted for the diet and lifestyle changes alone. I lost 90 pounds in 18 months by following a Mediterranean diet with emphasis on high quality protein. All of my blood and lipid markers are now within the reference ranges. I feel immeasurably guilty and remorseful for the foods I developed that have made our society less healthy. I encourage everyone to follow the advice in this video. Eat minimally processed foods…mostly low carb fruits, vegetables and more eggs, chicken and seafood — mostly fatty fish that are low in mercury. I am so sorry.

neutral.text: I'm age 24 and did gymnastics for 14 years from age 4. In Ukrainian national training we trained our bodies hard most days of the week. From maybe age 7 or 8 I trained my abdominals maybe daily and sometimes more than 1 time a day. We had strength training coach and he wanted us all to have extremely strong core muscles. I don't know where exercise addiction fits in your story but I saw some gymnasts like me had exercise addiction. I was raised in the orphanage system and boys homes. Life for me was stressful--as you say about internal stresses. I used abdominal exercising to cope with stress. When adopted and raised in America at age 12 I had a lot more stresses--using English all the time was tiring. I was homeschooled to age 15 then put into high school. Life in high school was tough and in rural schools the kids didn't know what to do with a boy in gymnastics. When I was almost age 16 some older athletes found me alone and decided to have fun beating me up. They held me in a full nelson and punched the shit out of my abdominals. They saw I had very muscular abdominals but didn't know that it turns out I can take a lot of hard punches. I was lucky I trained hard in Ukraine and kept going. I didn't handle stress well until maybe age 20. I now work in Construction full time and still keep training hard but not too insane. I lift weights 4 days a week and train abdominals in some serious way 5-6 days a week. My stress has gone down a lot. I never ran growing up but have been doing more running. I'm still not loving it but I don't hate it. Life is a lot better and feel I have the results I like. I'm 5'9" and weigh 178 pounds. I have less than 10% body fat which I think is my phenotype. And also gymnast pride in me has me wanting deeply muscled abdominals with no body fat. But that's not hard to do as I don't eat crazy amounts of calories.

Life in high school was tough and in rural schools the kids didn't know what to do with a boy in gymnastics. When I was almost age 16 some older athletes found me alone and decided to have fun beating me up. They held me in a full nelson and punched the shit out of my abdominals. They saw I had very muscular abdominals but didn't know that it turns out I can take a lot of hard punches. I was lucky I trained hard in Ukraine and kept going. I didn't handle stress well until maybe age 20. I now work in Construction full time and still keep training hard but not too insane. I lift weights 4 days a week and train abdominals in some serious way 5-6 days a week. My stress has gone down a lot. I never ran growing up but have been doing more running. I'm still not loving it but I don't hate it. Life is a lot better and feel I have the results I like. I'm 5'9" and weigh 178 pounds. I have less than 10% body fat which I think is my phenotype. And also gymnast pride in me has me wanting deeply muscled abdominals with no body fat. But that's not hard to do as I don't eat crazy amounts of calories.

positive.author: @MichaelJensen-g6i
positive.text: I liked and subscribed! I'm on 10 meds and have neuropathy but thought I had it due to heredity or some other reason not identifiable. I quit budesonide inhaler and got my voice back. They really tried to push gabapentin but I got the forewarning from my mother being prescribed it. I lost my mother as she was more than sleeping it was like she was unconscious. I took action and stopped it and she returned to normal. The pharmacist had a 90 day supply for me ready and at the counter I withheld and said I didn't want to waste it and take it home just reject it at the counter. Wow did she get into you must have it mode. I thought maybe if I don't take it they will label me non-compliant and put red flags around my name so now 7 years later I still have the three big bottles of it but will never use it. I still have neuropathy and need to figure out how as I didn't realize there are other meds that cause it. I'm 72 and wonder with so many meds if maybe I have shortened my life. I commute by bicycle and had one heart attack and a stent placed. Thanks for this video! I have rosuvastatin 5mg and Imdur 200mg a vaso-dialator... My phramacologist just said she sees some on 30 meds and do fine so no help there!
positive.label: Positive

positive.text:
i used to struggle with sleep alot. i have tried various supplements and they do work to a certain extend only. 
recently I made it mandatory to walk under the sun first thing in the morning for 15 minutes minimum. i do it barefoot and half naked. 

i also stopped drinking coffee and substituted with oolong tea. 

other protocols like zone 2 running, 15 minute sauna and meditating for 20-60mins before bed has helped me tremendously as well.

on super cloudy days and rain, i take vit d3(5000IU) + k2.

other supplements i take include omega 3, L carnitine, Benfotiamine, magnesium and L theanine. of which i only take omega 3 daily and the rest occasionally. 

if you have severe sleep problems i recommend L reuteri yogurt and magnesium glycinate + apigenin (at bed time).

Edit: disclaimer im not a medical doctor, each of us are unique- our enviornments, age, gender, genes may vary. we react to different substances differently. so please please please do your research and consult with your doctor before starting out any protocol. this is not to cover my back its to make sure you feel safe!

negative.author: @edwinGuyle
negative.text:
Dr. Brewer has been talking about CIMT for a while, long before it was FDA approved, and he explains the lifestyle choices that help prevent "sticky arteries." I feel like this sudden bombardment of cardiology industry trained professionals in social media is just industry "damage control." 

I watch my grandfather do what he was told for 30 years and he was waiting to die for his last 30 years of his life. 

Most of what I heard during this video, was not only should you "trust me bro, to manage your heart health," and you should also send us your kids, so we can manage their entire life of healthcare as well.

I didn't hear much in the way of self care, outside of "don't use tobacco products." We all knew that already.

neutral.author: @AliceR27
neutral.text: Never had a CTA, but been on statins since my 40s (now 67yo). When I look at my cholesterol levels, statins never affected my LDL at all. So a year ago I cut Crestor 20mg a day to 10mg, then 10mg a day to every other day, now twice a week. No difference. I did go low carb & back to gym. My triglycerides dropped 40%, but nothing else except slightly higher HDL, still LDL 120-130 & ApoB steady at 104. Had a CAC score of 52 in LAD 4yr ago (others 0). Such a quandry as far as what to do as I'm afraid lowering LDL to 30 with Repatha is too low. I've heard quotes for cardiac CT with AI is more like $2500+, not $1000, and I'm on Medicare now.

positive.author: @truthbetold6496
positive.text: This is by far the best advice i have received in many years, i cut down my training to a push pull leg 3 times per week, sometimes i take 48h between workout and hit every muscles once per week. I switch my exercise got a trap bar, front squats, i still lift heavy, doing 3 to 5 reps, and cut out all junk volume, also eat more protein. WOW the difference and i have more energy working out this way then was i was doing 5-6 workouts per week. You need to work hard, i keep 2 reps in the tank and protect your back and knees a good training belt, knee wraps, etc. No ego lifting
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @2Rugrats9597
positive.text:
I am 61, train one body part per week.
I workout 4 days a week.
When i workout i don’t go to fatigue, i leave two in the tank and give plenty of time to recover my connective tissue, nervous system and muscle. No overtraining, no fatigue, no pain. I do 8-12 reps w 4 sets each w one second concentric w a 3-4 second eccentric. I love the growth and the way things have been going w progress. Love your videos and appreciate what you do for us
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @perserverance333
positive.text: Rest is King. Train major muscle groups just once a week!
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @littlemoo52
positive.text:
Push, Pull, Legs, off day, Upper, Lower, off day.
Repeat.
It’s not easy in your 50’s but make sure you get your sleep and nutrition.  Take an extra day here and there. If you are overly sore go lighter with higher reps.  Know your body and recovery capabilities.

positive.text:
Hello everyone and thank you for watching! I really hope you found this video useful. I read all of your comments and try to reply to as many as I can every day across the channel. The community on this channel is absolutely fantastic.... people sharing their stories, supporting each other, and learning together. It's amazing to see. 

It means a lot to me that this has become a space where people are interested in the simple things that keep us healthy and prevent problems before they ever reach the hospital. If there’s a topic you’d like me to explain in a future video, please let me know in the comments.

If you’d like to support me, the best thing you can do is click the like button and subscribe. It really helps these videos reach more people who might benefit from them, and it allows me to keep making them! 

My goal with these videos is simple: to help as many people as possible stay healthier and avoid ending up in the emergency department if we can. 

Wishing you all the best, and thanks again!

Dr Alex 😊

positive.author: @paddydunne774
positive.text: Love your work Coach. Always fascinating to read the replies in the comments. They are always well thought through and, on a human level, thoughtful. It’s much appreciated. I’m an older rider who still to this day, think Jeff Spence’s Total Training for Motocross, is one of the most groundbreaking training manuals. The last three and years I have returned to the gym, mainly for my overall health and fitness. But I find lifting heavy on a hard training day, improves my riding as long as I have managed my sleep and nutrition sensibly. I still do a hard manual job on the farm, also. Feel blessed to still have the opportunity to be able to choose that lifestyle. I love the training partner I have become. But man do I miss that 19 year old self, slinging a leg over my 81 490 Maico. Not a care in the world 😉🤘👊
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @CraigHelgerson
positive.text: You have brilliant insights Rob. I was going to apply for my pro license in 1980 when a low speed tip over in practice blew my acl/mcl. An experiment reconstruction failed, so I left my love at the alter and went off to college. I ignored the sport for 40 some years, and when I came  back, I saw suspension had so advanced that the riders are not experiencing the brutal pounding that we experienced in the late 70s. We always flat landed everything and you would land so brutally hard your eyes would temporarily lose focus. A few years ago I saw a European fighter punching metal with little on his fists, I was convinced he had been hit in the head too many times until I learned that hard impacts to our bones strengthen them. I am not suggesting these kids do that but I would suggest far more seat time and build there whole bodies and hearts to race their motos without severe fatigue. Also, I would have rolled my eyes a few years ago if I heard what I'm about to say but if these have been put on any antibiotics in their lives, I learned that they have leaky gut where their food is not rebuilding their muscles as God designed them. I took high priced pre and probiotics and it helped a little albut then I learned that of all things kim chi has over 900 different bacteria. Within two weeks I found everything changed in the strength I would get from my workouts.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @ArnoldJudasRimmer
positive.text: Thank you for this video. It's so frustrating seeing other so called fitness experts telling dirt bike riders to do single leg bosu ball kettle bell deadlifts with 25 pounds in order to "get stronger" for racing.   I've been doing proper strength training for 18 months (405lb squat, 440lb DL, 250lb bench) and my endurance on the bike is so much better now. I'm still fat and old and not very good but I enjoy it more and have had some surprise results out of it.

neutral.author: @NathanMorey-z2f
neutral.text:
Love the great insight Coach, I went pro in Hard Enduro 2 years ago in Aus, and found even being one of the fittest on the grid that it didn't translate as well as the guys that got more seat time each week, where they saved more energy, through energy saving in techniques (alot harder to get the same seat time as them due to work and location).

I then also upped my stength training and HIIT and maintained a really high VO2 in the off season, I have taken alot of my training and fueling techniques from AFL players and triathletes, a combination of getting my fueling right and not breaking into my zone 4-5 HR to early in the race, has allowed me to go from burning out at about the 3-4 hour mark to now the 12-16 hours of riding before musclar fatigue. I also worked alot on balance and plyometric exercises and found this translated directly to the bike and allowed for much more overall bike control and minimised injuries.

I would be very interested to hear what you would suggest for racers doing events such as Romaniacs/Dakar or the likes where there are 4 days in a row of hard racing, or even in Hard Enduro having a 3 hour qualifying followed by the race the day after, I tend to notice alot of racers burn out on the second day much more.
