positive.author: @wfqsfg
positive.text:
I am 69 also. Will turn 70 in a few months. I started back working out after about 10-12 years of being a retired couch potato. I was quite active in my early years. Jogging, weightlifting, pickup basketball and other sports. 
I started back about 8 months ago and had plenty of muscle and joint soreness to start. Most of that is gone now. I still get muscle soreness when I pump up the volume. But I am experienced and I know when I tear down muscle I will have soreness. I walk now instead of jogging and lift weights. I will ride my bicycle when winter is over. I cleaned up my eating and try real hard to get the protein in that I need, especially when weightlifting. I've lost 30lbs since starting back with 20 more to go to reach my goal. I have plateaued and have to figure out how to get past that. 
Reading the other comments I would like to say I supplement fiber. I wouldn't want to be without it. I try to get enough in with meals but that doesn't always happen. 
I would like to tell people my own age,  just walk every day!! If you don't want to do anything else, at least walk!! Watch videos on YouTube on some tips but walking is something most can do.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @archaeobard1
positive.text: Great advice! I'm trying to get my cousin's wife (who is 61) to eat like this as she is having problems with falling and her hips - she needs to start the process for hip replacement. She broke her hip when she was 13 and it's starting to cause her serious issues, but she's basically said she is getting old and this stuff just happens. For a start, 61 is nowhere near old! She's staggering around like she is 90, stooped over, and grabbing hold of things. She's rapidly losing muscle. I think I've convinced her to at least go and see her dr, but she is lacking 'the willingness', as you say, to help herself.
positive.label: Positive

negative.text:
I had an unscheduled hospital visit thanks to anaphylaxis, during which point it was determined I was in a state of ketoacidosis  because I had 5.5mmol/L ketones AND my blood sugar was so HIGH (AROUND 20MMOL/L - a direct result of the intravenous adrenaline and steroid shots)

They wanted me on intravenous insulin!  

Idiots!

I told them that wouldn't be necessary, that upon withdrawal of adrenaline they'd see my blood sugars go back down to around 2.5-3mmol/L. And, yes, when that happened 17 hours later (yes, I was in intravenous adrenaline for 17 straight hours - NOT recommended) General Medicine (who accepted me into Resus before transferring my to ICU) tried to hold an intervention to have my driver's licence rescinded etc...

Thankfully, the ICU Dr understood therapeutic ketosis...


But it's such a mine field out there, with so few medical professionals understanding, and even less who want to listen to the patient! 

To think an untrained patient could know more about their own body that the trained doctor!

positive.text:
I am 79 going 80 years old was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, had a knee replacement and two stents. I was advised by my good doctor that I was heading to the airport.he said put the handbrake on. Stop eating sugar and exercise, I stopped drinking alcohol cut out carbohydrates and exercise in gym classes every day except weekends..
I have lost 32 kilograms over four years and am no longer in the diabetic range, normal cholesterol, normal HbA1c, normal liver function and am fitter than I was at age 50
No bread, pasta, pastry, potatoes sweet Corn, no sugar drinks or fruit juicers.
I can vouch that a life style change not reliance on medication can help or fully reverse this cycle. I adopt a positive attitude to taking care of my blood sugars..it certainly made a huge difference in a very short time.
I Thank you for your most valuable advice on fruit, diabetes sufferers are in need of logic to assist with food choices, your dedication to your profession is greatly appreciated

positive.text: Dr. Kent, this is hands down the most clear and practical guide on fruit and diabetes I’ve ever seen! 🍎✨ As someone who wants to understand real nutrition without all the confusing fear-mongering, your breakdown of Glycemic Index (GI) versus Glycemic Load (GL) is an absolute game-changer. 🤯 It’s so empowering to learn that we don't have to fear fruit, but simply need to manage it smartly. Thank you, Jesus!

positive.author: @PatientAdvocateHelp
positive.text:
Great video.  The reason walking helps so much is that it helps move the lymphatic system. This is especially important in chronically ill patients. The lymphatic system is now being shown in new research to be an important organ in fat loss especially as it relates to systemic inflammation. 

Another issue that you should address is the chronic consumption of C15 fatty acid.  This is a product that should only cycled. The reason it helps and or can acutely improve health issues is that it polarizes your macrophages to M2. This is the anti-inflammatory pathway.  A low carb ketogenic diet and glucocorticoids also polarize the macrophages to M2. Studies now show chronic polarization of macrophages to M1 or M2 eventually develops insulin resistance even in lean fit individuals.  

Whereas, most long chain fatty acids polarize macrophages to M1, C15 polarizes the macrophages to M2. I believe future studies will eventually show chronic intake of C15 may be detrimental to health. However, acute intake and cycling said nutritional supplement is fantastic. 

There is also some early research indicating possible issues of creating endoplasmic reticulum stress. While I haven’t thoroughly investigated said issues, this could be a potential issue.

neutral.author: @SirPatrickStar
neutral.text:
1	Mobility that only works without load – 0:00–1:45 Good bodyweight movement breaks down when weight is added. Reverse it: Train mobility under load to build true functional range and stability.
	2	Inability to hang from a bar for sufficient time – 1:45–3:05 Tests grip strength, shoulder mobility, and core control. Reverse it: Hang daily; progress to 2+ minutes (men) or 90+ seconds (women).
	3	Can’t touch or overlap hands behind your back – 3:05–4:55 Poor shoulder internal/external rotation. Reverse it: Use broomstick-assisted stretches and doorway slides.
	4	Low VO₂ max – 4:55–6:40 Strong predictor of cardiovascular decline and mortality. Reverse it: Perform HIIT 1–2× per week (e.g., 30 sec all-out + 90 sec easy, 6–8 rounds).
	5	Chronic dehydration – 6:40–8:20 Affects cognition, energy, joints, and performance. Reverse it: Drink ~¾ of body weight (lbs) in ounces daily; use a marked bottle with rubber bands to track.
	6	Not supplementing with creatine monohydrate – 8:20–9:55 Impacts muscle preservation, strength, and emerging brain health benefits. Reverse it: Take 5–10 g daily (no cycling needed).
	7	Ignoring physical weaknesses – 9:55–11:20 Avoiding uncomfortable movements creates imbalances and limits progress. Reverse it: Dedicate part of every workout to movements you dislike or suck at.
	8	Not training to true failure – 11:20–13:40 Stopping short of real failure reduces stimulus for muscle and strength gains. Reverse it: Push sets to actual failure (while managing overall volume).
	9	Skipping corrective exercises – 13:40–15:15 Neglecting stabilizers and weak links leads to compensations and injury. Reverse it: Regularly include face pulls, rotator cuff work, hip mobility drills, etc.
	10	Relying exclusively on machines (avoiding free weights) – 15:15–17:45 Misses stabilizer engagement and real-world coordination. Reverse it: Prioritize barbells, dumbbells, and bodyweight for most training.
	11	Not prioritizing protein as you age – 17:45–20:40 Age-related muscle loss lowers metabolism and appetite. Reverse it: Aim for 1–1.2 g protein per lb body weight; include it in every meal and use shakes if needed.
	12	No direct ab/core training – 20:40–22:20 Compound lifts alone don’t fully develop the entire core. Reverse it: Train core directly every day (5–10 min) with anti-rotation, extension, and rotation control exercises.
	13	Jumping straight to pharmaceutical interventions – 22:20–26:45 Using TRT, peptides, or GLP-1 drugs as first-line options instead of optimizing basics. Reverse it: Exhaust training, nutrition, sleep, and recovery first; use meds only when truly needed and under medical supervision.
	14	Poor lateral stability (failing the elevated-leg side plank test) – 26:45–end Inability to hold a side plank with top leg raised for 30 seconds reveals weak glute medius and frontal-plane control. Reverse it: Practice elevated-leg side planks; build up to 30 seconds per side.
Implementing even a few of these changes consistently can dramatically improve both lifespan and quality of life as you age

What if some forms of depression (at least those associated with visceral fat) are an evolutionary adaptation to help humans slow down and consume less food. You'd still be hungry while depressed, but the depression itself would inhibit excess calorie consumption. 
Wild speculation over.

neutral.author: @OperatorGnosisRecords
neutral.text:
Great convo. The alcohol part at around 2hrs.23 is very important, as I think Huby is a little biased against alcohol. This guy gives a great perspective on why and how mild social drinking might be a net positive IF you're system has the resources to allocate to the cost of detoxifying it (which, for instance, many young people, and fit, happy, secure older people, will have). Superb. My Grandad lived until he was 101, and he had one small sherry every single night. I suspect the cost of the booze on his system was outweighed by the relaxing ritual of it, as stress is potentially more costly to mitochondrial health than one small drink. He was utterly a man of moderation in every aspect of life, very ordered, happily married, didn't concern himself with the stresses of the world, was a high ranking police officer, and never over ate, or drank heavily.  So his one small sherry probably never outweighed all of that. 

I think you can look at various 'indulgences' in this light. Especially as so many of them are tied to our sense of self, and our sentimental connection to our past. Determining how much you want to allocate to technically unhealthy, but subjectively fun, and potentially stress reducing behaviours, is an excellent way to look at things. With that being said, though, most people who are metabolically unhealthy (which might be a majority these days, at least in the US and the UK) are likely somewhat in that state BECAUSE they lean too much on indulgences, and not enough on improving mitochondrial health through diet, exercise, sleep optimisation etc etc. In which case, less, or no, booze is a better option.

Do reduce it to the right star in a friendly neighborhood and the right sized planet in a stable habitable orbit gives you a much better estimate. This reduces the number of possiblities to reasonable number.  It also tells you SETI is a complete waste one you have eliminated stars within a few lightyears away.  Even a one message sent and received a decade apart is pretty worthless.  Plus traveling even one light year is a death sentence.

positive.author: @YourIdentityIsAHoax
positive.text:
This episode quietly dismantles a very modern illusion:

We live like we’re disembodied minds who just “think positive,” while eating ultra-processed food, nuking our microbes with antibiotics, and wondering why our mood, focus, and willpower feel broken.

The gut isn’t just about digestion, it’s a regulatory environment for the psyche. A chronically inflamed microbiome doesn’t just give you GI issues, it warps your emotional baseline,  irritability, brain fog, low resilience, overreactions in relationships.

It’s funny: people talk about “working on themselves” while completely ignoring the ecosystem that’s modulating their neurotransmitters 24/7.

Identity, behavior, even what we think is “free will” looks different when you realize how much is being negotiated by organisms you never see.

This intersection between biology, identity and behavior is exactly what I explore on my channel lately

negative.text: I’ve been on carvedilol for a little over 2 years.  I’ve been looking for the way off for 2 years.  I’m a retired doctor of 34 years in practice. When my BP went down to 90/58 after exercising my cardiologists answering service got back to me two days later and told me to cut my carvedilol dose in half.  Duh!  That’s what I had already done.  I already do most of the things you mentioned, but some in supplement form.  I am going to try to do them all from food (in steps) substituting the real thing for supplements.  Some things that have also helped is drinking oolong tea and eating a clove of garlic. Oolong tea has twice the EGCG of green tea and garlic blocks the prostaglandins (PGE5) both preventing the LDL from becoming oxidized and attaching to the artery wall and causing atherosclerosis.

positive.author: @SeniorBeWell
positive.text: This is one of the most important messages seniors need to hear. Walking alone does not fix poor leg circulation after 60. As a physical therapist, I see this every week, people doing everything right, walking daily, elevating legs, wearing compression socks, yet still dealing with swelling, cold feet, and balance problems. The calf muscle pump is the real driver of circulation, and this video explains it clearly and correctly. The emphasis on controlled calf holds and time under tension is exactly what restores blood flow and reduces fall risk. If you are over 60 and worried about your legs, this is not optional information, it is essential.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @StrongSeniors365
positive.text: This really changed how I think about leg circulation after 60. I used to believe walking alone was enough, yet the swelling and cold feet never fully improved. Adding these simple, focused movements made me feel warmer, steadier, and more confident on my feet over time. It’s encouraging to see how small, intentional exercises can protect independence and spark meaningful conversations about aging stronger together.

negative.text:
So glad to hear Layne touch on some of the "predatory marketing" around age and sex. The idea that menopausal women NEED to train differently or can't do certain things has become kind of weirdly insidious. Same thing for guys and aging, like the whole "men over 40"  thing.

Like Layne said, obviously there are considerations with age and sex - so it's not to say there's nothing there in regard to what's being marketed. But as a 36 year old guy, I constantly find my mind going to this place of "I've only got 4 years left till I'm 40 and then it's all downhill from there...I better pack on as much muscle now while I can." 

And while that may still be a good thing to do, it kinda sucks that my mind just sort of automatically defaults to 40 years old being some kind of hard cutoff age for men and building muscle. Takes away joy in the idea of simply training for life and not ascribing the bummer factor of what training should look like at certain ages.

positive.text:
I'm 59 and my husband is 61. We have been taking the following vitamins over and above the meds were are prescribed for at least the  last 5 years: Vitamin D3 (actually prescribed to me), Vitamin K2 (but not combined into one pill), low dose aspirin, fish oil, and B-Complex. I also take collagen peptides. My husband takes NAD and I will be starting it as well soon. Besides, I was told that if you do not have a deficiency in your blood work, there's no need to take a supplement of it. Magnesium is one of them. I do not have any of the symptoms you mention that a low Magnesium level would present.

4 vitamins NOT to take:
--Vitamin A
--Iron
--Calcium
--Vitamin B6

4 vitamins to take:
--Magnesium
--Vitamin D3
--Vitamin K2
--Omega 3's

positive.author: @chai7501
positive.text: Re how viewing bright light a couple of hours before sleep disrupts the sleeping pattern. Circadian rhythm regulation is really key to all aspects of health, yet it is all too often overlooked. Many people have bright screens near their eyes at night, unaware of the disruption that is causing their body clocks. Avoiding bright light near the eyes, a couple of hours before bedtime, is essential for sleep, as is having darkness during sleep, as both allow the brain to make the sleep hormone melatonin. Viewing light close to waking up in the morning is essential for alertness and energy.  We evolved to have circadian rhythm that follows the light / dark cycle of day and night,  and these light /dark signals reach the brain via the eyes, which are actually part of the brain. For anyone living in the Northern hemisphere or who has to be up before the sun is, highly recommend getting a SAD lamp to wake the brain up in the morning, the difference it can make is amazing.

all.author: @chai7501
all.text: Re how viewing bright light a couple of hours before sleep disrupts the sleeping pattern. Circadian rhythm regulation is really key to all aspects of health, yet it is all too often overlooked. Many people have bright screens near their eyes at night, unaware of the disruption that is causing their body clocks. Avoiding bright light near the eyes, a couple of hours before bedtime, is essential for sleep, as is having darkness during sleep, as both allow the brain to make the sleep hormone melatonin. Viewing light close to waking up in the morning is essential for alertness and energy.  We evolved to have circadian rhythm that follows the light / dark cycle of day and night,  and these light /dark signals reach the brain via the eyes, which are actually part of the brain. For anyone living in the Northern hemisphere or who has to be up before the sun is, highly recommend getting a SAD lamp to wake the brain up in the morning, the difference it can make is amazing.

positive.author: @JestonyNatindim
positive.text: I spent a long time trying to think my way out of brain fog before I realized the problem was blood flow, not willpower. In severe hypothyroidism, global cerebral blood flow can drop by nearly 40 percent. The brain operates on a strict energy budget, and when metabolism drops, complex cognition and memory are the first to be cut — the abandoned neurons theory. The solution is not a nootropic. It's restoring the metabolic supply line. That shift in understanding was what finally pointed me in the right direction.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @YourOrganizedAuntie
positive.text: Oh goodness, the moment you said “brain fog, fatigue, inflammation, and the mineral deficiency no one talks about,” my whole spirit perked up like “Ah yes, the plot twist of adulthood,” because whew, I once went through a season where I was so tired I thought my soul had low battery. I’d walk into a room and forget why I was there, then argue with myself like “Luise, focus… no seriously, what are we doing here?” and my brain would just shrug. And here’s the wild part: it wasn’t burnout, it wasn’t stress, it wasn’t even my questionable sleep schedule. It was a mineral deficiency so sneaky it should honestly be on the FBI watchlist. When I finally got it checked, the doctor looked at me like “Ma’am, your cells are basically running on dial‑up internet,” and I nearly fainted. And oh wow, once I started replenishing it, the fog lifted so fast I thought I had unlocked a cheat code. Suddenly I could think clearly, communicate like a functioning adult, and even my productivity came back from the dead like “Hey girl, miss me?” It taught me something hilarious and humbling: sometimes you’re not unmotivated, you’re just biochemically confused. And the moment your body gets what it’s been begging for, everything shifts. Your energy stabilizes, your mood stops doing gymnastics, and your brain finally stops feeling like a browser with 47 tabs open. Honestly, if anyone’s been feeling “off” for no reason, it might not be vibes… it might be minerals quietly screaming for help.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text: Wonderful episode Andrew. Terry is so right: addiction is a substitute for relationship (I am now 44 years sober). positive.text:
#7 - Kiwi (golden variety): Contains lutein, zeaxanthin, and serotonin for better sleep
#6 - Watermelon: Rich in lycopene; supports hydration and blood flow
#5 - Black currants: High in anthocyanins for night vision and blood flow to optic nerve
#4 - Blueberries (wild/frozen): Contains pterostilbene for photoreceptor protection
#3 - Dragon fruit (red-fleshed): Betalains support oxygen delivery to retina
#2 - Goji berries: Highest dietary source of zeaxanthin for macular protection
#1 - Papaya ⭐
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @andreafong9952
positive.text: 7. Two golden Kiwis scooped with inner edge. 6. Watermelon with some white rind-1-2 cups. White rind can be pickled or blended into a smoothie. 5. Black Currents 50 milligrams or as an extract daily 4. Wild Blueberries usually found frozen 1/3 cup before bed. Freeze and thaw to eat 1 hour before bed. 3.  Dragon fruit-red only. 1/2 red fruit. Chew seeds don’t swallow whole. 2. Gogi berries soak 2 tablespoon dried berries in warm water. Eat 1/2 hour before bed. Pairs with small square of 85% cacao. 1. Papaya 1 cup ripe cubes room temperature fresh papaya before bed. Squeeze fresh lime over papaya. No dairy or high calcium foods with fruits. Add a small amount of fat. 2-3 walnuts or other healthy fat. No scrubbing only Pat clean right before eating and eat at room temperature. Eat no earlier than 90-60 minutes before bed. Video has additional tips that are important and not mentioned here.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text: Until I was 5 1/2 I was far sighted.  Then my dad let me go down a snow hill in Minnesota by myself.  I got halfway down and didn't realize I couldn't steer and my sled hit the brick building, and I got a concussion, in the middle of my forehead, and two black eyes.  My mother was furious with my dad for letting me go down alone. At some point, my eyes stabilized after that accident.  Then when I was 8, I became near sided.   I'm 78 now and living in Oregon.  The last time I got my driver's license I passed without glass as my near sidedness was getting better all the time.   Life is crazy sometimes that is for sure.

positive.author: @michaelevans9675
positive.text: I started doing something 2 1/2 years ago and I am not a exercise science major or a personal trainer like you. But this has worked for me. I tried the one meal a day which is more of a spiritual thing for me as a Christian to pray And I also tried the keto type thing and I also tried the intermittent fasting thing. Those didn’t work for me. What I tried is what I called the chainsaw diet. I’m metabolism was like an old chainsaw that was rusty in the garage and need new spark plugs and I couldn’t get it started. So basically what I started to do at first was eat about eight meals a day every hour and a half small meals, lots of vegetables, lean proteins, nuts and fruit and then I would eat about one regular meal a day out of those seven. Now I usually do five meals a day and do one regular meal a day for the most part. This is paired with regular exercise, including going to the gym to lift weights, at least four times a week and drinking lots of water. I had tried going to the gym for three or four years, but I never really saw results because I never got my diet in Check The bottom line is you can’t outwork a bad diet. Now that I’m stuck with this plan, it really works for me. I’ve essentially jumpstarted my metabolism and I’ve kept it there. When I eat too much, drink too much beer or eat too much bad food I will start to have stomach problems and gain a little bit of weight and then I will correct. Essentially get up in the morning eat something lean drink some water. Make sure you get enough protein workout And don’t overheat. And then just listen to your body. You’ll see results I’ve seen a lot. I was always skinny and lean and I got up to 210 pounds because of bad diet and getting older and losing my metabolism at age 35. Now I’m almost 43 and I’m sitting at about 160 to 170 consistently. Plus, I’m leaner and I have more muscle. I’m not as cut as this gentleman because I don’t have a really really clean diet, but I’m certainly much better off and much healthier than I was before.
positive.label: Positive

There is one massively major problem with OMAD, and that is, there is almost no way that you can get your total daily protein requirements in one meal. Even if you could get 150 to 200 g of protein in one meal, your body would not likely be able to metabolize and incorporate a significant portion of that.

Therefore, since you are unlikely to get enough protein, a fairly significant portion of the weight that is lost is likely to be lean muscle mass.

all.author: @michaelevans9675
all.text: I started doing something 2 1/2 years ago and I am not a exercise science major or a personal trainer like you. But this has worked for me. I tried the one meal a day which is more of a spiritual thing for me as a Christian to pray And I also tried the keto type thing and I also tried the intermittent fasting thing. Those didn’t work for me. What I tried is what I called the chainsaw diet. I’m metabolism was like an old chainsaw that was rusty in the garage and need new spark plugs and I couldn’t get it started. So basically what I started to do at first was eat about eight meals a day every hour and a half small meals, lots of vegetables, lean proteins, nuts and fruit and then I would eat about one regular meal a day out of those seven. Now I usually do five meals a day and do one regular meal a day for the most part. This is paired with regular exercise, including going to the gym to lift weights, at least four times a week and drinking lots of water. I had tried going to the gym for three or four years, but I never really saw results because I never got my diet in Check The bottom line is you can’t outwork a bad diet. Now that I’m stuck with this plan, it really works for me. I’ve essentially jumpstarted my metabolism and I’ve kept it there. When I eat too much, drink too much beer or eat too much bad food I will start to have stomach problems and gain a little bit of weight and then I will correct. Essentially get up in the morning eat something lean drink some water. Make sure you get enough protein workout And don’t overheat. And then just listen to your body. You’ll see results I’ve seen a lot. I was always skinny and lean and I got up to 210 pounds because of bad diet and getting older and losing my metabolism at age 35. Now I’m almost 43 and I’m sitting at about 160 to 170 consistently. Plus, I’m leaner and I have more muscle. I’m not as cut as this gentleman because I don’t have a really really clean diet, but I’m certainly much better off and much healthier than I was before.

positive.author: @shteebo
positive.text:
The most important step for health/fitness is adopting a sustainable diet that moves you toward a healthy weight and keeps you there.   For me, that's keto with intermittent fasting (meal skipping).   Then add a form of exercise with low risk of injury.  For me, it was walking.  I made excellent progress in just a couple months on both weight management and basic fitness with just those steps.   Adding daily push-ups and air squats is great preparation for a resistance program.

The problem with jumping into resistance training prior to establishing basic fitness is it's so easy to overdo and suffer injury or debilitating soreness.  I found it's better to establish a routine of movement prior to focusing on strength.  This naturally introduces the "good burn" feeling where you're only mildly sore and stretching feels really good.  You'll know your resistance workouts are leveled appropriately when you wake up feeling the good burn.

all.author: @shteebo
all.text:
The most important step for health/fitness is adopting a sustainable diet that moves you toward a healthy weight and keeps you there.   For me, that's keto with intermittent fasting (meal skipping).   Then add a form of exercise with low risk of injury.  For me, it was walking.  I made excellent progress in just a couple months on both weight management and basic fitness with just those steps.   Adding daily push-ups and air squats is great preparation for a resistance program.

The problem with jumping into resistance training prior to establishing basic fitness is it's so easy to overdo and suffer injury or debilitating soreness.  I found it's better to establish a routine of movement prior to focusing on strength.  This naturally introduces the "good burn" feeling where you're only mildly sore and stretching feels really good.  You'll know your resistance workouts are leveled appropriately when you wake up feeling the good burn.

positive.author: @maireadweaver8952
positive.text: I am Irish and we have a public healthcare system here which, whilst broken in many places and has a LOT wrong with it, at least people can get healthcare without bankrupting themselves. Our GP system is under huge stress with a shortage of GPs and an increasing population, HOWEVER, even though you may be waiting a couple of weeks for non-emergency appointments, you can still establish a good relationship and have regular check-ups within the system. Whenever I have travelled to the US I have been completely shocked that no-one I met actually has a GP that they see regularly. On the handful of occasions, whilst in the US, where we needed a GP/afterhours GP for mild illness like allergic reactions to insect bites or a mislaid prescription, we were funnelled into an ER situation which seemed bonkers -  and such an unnecessary waste of ER staff time (not to mention how embarrassed we were going to an ER with such relatively trivial medical issues, and the consequent cost). In the absence of regular advice and follow-up treatments from a GP, in addition to the astronomical costs charged in the US, it is no wonder people resort to Dr Google/Gwynnie/Snake-oil salesmen. IMHO.
positive.label: Positive

all.text: I am Irish and we have a public healthcare system here which, whilst broken in many places and has a LOT wrong with it, at least people can get healthcare without bankrupting themselves. Our GP system is under huge stress with a shortage of GPs and an increasing population, HOWEVER, even though you may be waiting a couple of weeks for non-emergency appointments, you can still establish a good relationship and have regular check-ups within the system. Whenever I have travelled to the US I have been completely shocked that no-one I met actually has a GP that they see regularly. On the handful of occasions, whilst in the US, where we needed a GP/afterhours GP for mild illness like allergic reactions to insect bites or a mislaid prescription, we were funnelled into an ER situation which seemed bonkers -  and such an unnecessary waste of ER staff time (not to mention how embarrassed we were going to an ER with such relatively trivial medical issues, and the consequent cost). positive.text:
Hello everyone and thank you for watching! I really hope you found this video useful. I read all of your comments and try to reply to as many as I can every day across the channel. The community on this channel is absolutely fantastic.... people sharing their stories, supporting each other, and learning together. It's amazing to see. 

It means a lot to me that this has become a space where people are interested in the simple things that keep us healthy and prevent problems before they ever reach the hospital. If there’s a topic you’d like me to explain in a future video, please let me know in the comments.

If you’d like to support me, the best thing you can do is click the like button and subscribe. It really helps these videos reach more people who might benefit from them, and it allows me to keep making them! 

My goal with these videos is simple: to help as many people as possible stay healthier and avoid ending up in the emergency department if we can. 

Wishing you all the best, and thanks again!

Dr Alex 😊

positive.text: I'm practically in tears watching this. You nailed my biggest fear - being dependent. I'm in my early 60s and live alone. I have lived a pretty active lifestyle (runner, hiker, on-my-feet-all-day-teacher ) until the last few years following retirement. I can tell my body has declined significantly because even though I still workout regularly, I am not as active during the day - I sit too much. But listening to you, I feel like I can turn this around and get back on track before it becomes irreversible. Your videos carry so much important information for people of all ages. The words "thank you" are not enough.

Someone told me that walking is just maintenance,  but strength training will keep you independent. I think that's true.

negative.author: @biolbd
negative.text: Well said. A close relative was in good health, very active, spry, etc. until at age 87, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer. The decision was made (by some family members) to have him undergo proton radiation therapy, which caused massive problems with urinary incontinence, and curtailed a lot of his activities. He then entered into the sick care system: meds for the incontinence, meds for depression, meds for cholesterol, etc. Even had to go to a cardiologist despite having zero heart problems. By age 90, he began having neurological issues that resembled a form of Parkinson’s and is now in assisted living and severely depressed about his situation. He has lost the ability to swallow or talk well, and is confined to a wheelchair yet his mind is still sharp, so that makes his situation even worse. One wonders if he might have been better off living with the cancer until his death.

positive.author: @ARFF1Tampa
positive.text: Thank you. I stepped in to a gym for the first time in my life 12 months ago at age 63. Mostly for piece of mind (wasn't going to sit around and mope for 4 years) I hired a trainer for the first 4 months to learn, then took over on my own. I, pleasantly, got results I'd never imagined. Trainers and lifetime gym patrons came up to me with questions and compliments I'd never imagined.  "What are you doing to get those results?" ect. I went from 204 pounds 23 percent body fat, to 150 pounds and between 13 and 14.5 percent body fat. I, obviously, being inexperienced, over trained (as I went 5X a week for 3 hours a day (plus I play hockey 3X a week) but it really, made me happy, feel good every day, and was an escape from this disaste[R]. My only unfortunate result is the amount of fat you lose in your face, which changes your appearance (and, not for the better). 8 ounces of hot high quality coffee , add half teaspoon of ceylon cinnamon, 1 tablespoon unsweetened cocoa powder, 1 teaspoon of MTC oil, half a cup of organic milk or fortified soy milk, 1 scoop of unflavored collagen powder , 1 scoop of whey protein isolate, 1 teaspoon of ground chia seed powder, half a teaspoon of turmeric and a small pinch of black pepper. 
Blend all ingredients thoroughly using a milk frother or small blender to create a creamy delicious drink.

positive.author: @Mauseeqi
positive.text:
Summary 
In this video, presented by Dr. Richard Ben, discusses how simple adjustments to coffee consumption habits can help seniors and those with pre-diabetes naturally stabilize blood sugar levels and improve metabolic health. While coffee contains beneficial compounds like chlorogenic acid (2:48), improper timing and additives can spike cortisol and glucose levels.

### The Three Major Coffee Mistakes
1. Drinking on an empty stomach (5:23): Caffeine amplifies the body's natural morning cortisol spike, causing the liver to release extra glucose before you have even eaten.
2. Adding sugar or artificial sweeteners (6:32): Sugar causes immediate glucose spikes, while certain artificial sweeteners may negatively impact gut microbiota, hindering long-term blood sugar control.
3. Afternoon or evening consumption (7:54): Due to its long half-life, late-day caffeine can interfere with sleep, which is critical for glucose regulation.

### How to Optimize Your Coffee Routine
•	Morning Routine: Wait 30–60 minutes after waking, drink water first, and consume a protein-rich breakfast before your coffee (9:16).
•	Before Lunch: Drink a small cup of plain black coffee 20–30 minutes before your main meal to help control post-meal glucose absorption (10:31).
•	After Exercise: Drinking coffee within 30 minutes of physical activity can help muscles absorb glucose more efficiently (11:26).

### The "Protection Triad" for Metabolic Health
•	Smart Coffee: Plain, freshly ground coffee without sugar or artificial additives (15:57).
•	Movement: 30 minutes of moderate walking, 3–5 times per week (16:05).
•	Protein: Ensure a source of protein (e.g., eggs, cheese, fish) is included in every main meal (16:29).

positive.author: @gritsteel4559
positive.text: Thanks for the info, should help others a lot.  I on the other hand has become so used to coffee.  Since I got diabetes Type 2, I had to switch my coffee to only black coffee, no sugar.  Now, I hate coffee with sugar.  I drink a lot of coffee, about 4 to 5 cups a day, and I can't sleep if I don't drink coffee (but I also can't wake up without coffee nearby).  I was living a more sedentary lifestyle at that time, diabetes controlled well by medication and care in glucose intake.  Nowadays in my 60s, I do strength and muscle building training with some plyometrics in my 60s (just some dumbbells of different weights, a horizontal bar, and calisthenics, I don't need to pay gym fees), and I am getting hypos.  So I now try to eat more, with more protein, and have some good complex carbs and even simple carbs to balance it out, more like my pre-diabetes days except without sweet drinks like sodas which I learned to avoid.  I don't even check my blood sugar now, it's always Hba1c 5.7 to 5.8 after every 6 months visit to the hospital.  I guess I now believe the finding that building muscles will help a lot against diabetes, as "Increasing muscle mass improves insulin sensitivity, enhancing glucose tolerance and lowering blood sugar levels".  Walking or even running is not enough, imho,  although good for other stuff like cardio.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @SeniorStrength-us
positive.text: I’m 61 and I used to drink strong coffee first thing in the morning on an empty stomach, then wonder why I felt shaky, tired, and hungry again an hour later. After I started having breakfast first and stopped adding sugar to my coffee, my energy became much more stable and even my blood sugar numbers improved. It’s crazy how such a small habit can make such a big difference over time. Has anyone else noticed that the timing of their coffee changes how they feel during the day?

positive.author: @WoundstoWisdomBible
positive.text:
Here's a strange thing that came up in my CPTSD healing journey...
throughout my life, I've ALWAYS gone away by myself somewhere if Im really upset and know im going to cry. I could never show people i was upset but i thought it was normal behaviour until i was working on my healing and my mom told me that from infanthood i was allergic to the formula milk and would get terrible collic and be crying in pain. But she was told by the midwives back then, that i was just looking for attention when i was crying in pain, and to park me in the buggie at the end of the garden and let me cry it out alone. Now i realised why even as an adult, i would go cry alone because i learnt that no one cared enough to help when you are in pain and you just cry alone until you cant cry anymore. And when you are quiet you get to come back to everyone else. How sad to be trained that way and how something that repeatedly happened when you were too young to even remember it, gets hardwired into your nervous system and can effect you for the rest of your life, if you dont do the healing work. That was just one of MANY things that came up. Ive come a long way. Its not easy to do this because so many things come up and have to be worked through. Sometimes it felt like a never-ending rabbit hole. But now im feeling so much calmer, more aware, emotionally attuned, able to set boundaries, seeing other peoples behaviour as just that- their behaviour, not a reflection of my worth.

positive.author: @PerAsperaAdAstra8755
positive.text:
*Dr. Nick Norwitz's 7 Ways to Lower Blood Sugar (Without Cutting Carbs):*

1. *Post-Meal Walks:* Taking a 15–30 minute walk after eating activates glute-4 receptors in your muscles via an insulin-independent pathway. This allows your muscles to act as "glucose sponges," soaking up sugar directly from the bloodstream [01:13]

2. *Red Light Exposure:* Exposure to red and infrared light (including natural sunlight) can penetrate the skin to influence mitochondrial function and energy utilization, helping to stabilize blood glucose [03:06]

3. *Meal Sequencing:* The order in which you eat your food matters significantly. Eating *protein and fiber-rich vegetables before carbohydrates* can reduce the total blood sugar spike by as much as *73%* compared to eating the same foods in reverse order [03:42]

4. *Use a Continuous Glucose Monitor (CGM):* Individual responses to food vary wildly. Norwitz notes that some people spike higher from a banana than a cookie, or from kale than chocolate, due to personal inflammatory and glycemic responses. A CGM helps identify these unique triggers [04:41]

5. *Be Aware of Medications:* Some common drugs affect glucose metabolism. For instance, **statins** have been associated with long-term increases in HbA1c and may significantly reduce the hormone *GLP-1* (which helps regulate blood sugar) [05:35].
.
6. *Allulose as a Sweetener:* Allulose is a natural sugar that has negligible calories and does not spike blood sugar. When consumed with regular sugar, it can actually blunt the glycemic spike you would otherwise experience [07:23].

7. *Stress Management (Breathing/Meditation):* Stress activates the *medial amygdala,* which has a "direct wire" to the liver. This neural connection can trigger the liver to produce sugar immediately (bypassing cortisol and adrenaline), so reducing stress stops your body from manufacturing unnecessary sugar [08:19]

*The Key Takeaway:* Blood sugar management is about more than just what you eat; it's heavily influenced by *how* you eat, your physical activity, light exposure, and even your brain's direct control over liver function [09:01].

positive.author: @Murse_Darius
positive.text: In my experience, the walk has to be 30+ minutes, and can't be just a casual stroll. You don't need to power walk, but it needs to be somewhat like how people walk on the sidewalks of a big city. Like you have somewhere to be. If you stop too early, though, you'll often still get a rise. If you want to completely flatten the spike, 45 min will do the trick. Also, you don't have to walk. The soleus muscle in the calf is one of the most glucose hungry muscles in the body. So even if you stand in place, like when you're washing dishes and just do calf raises, it works. (I've done this very experiment myself).

neutral.author: @PhoenixWoody
neutral.text:
Here is my quick Grok confirmation about Vitamin D: 
What part of the body triggers Vitamin D production?

The skin is the part of the body that triggers and carries out vitamin D production. When ultraviolet B (UVB) rays from sunlight (wavelength 290–320 nm) hit the skin, they convert 7-dehydrocholesterol (a cholesterol derivative naturally present in the epidermis) into previtamin D₃. This previtamin D₃ then spontaneously isomerizes into vitamin D₃ (cholecalciferol) through a temperature-dependent process in the skin itself.

Key points for accuracy:
Production happens primarily in the epidermis, especially the stratum spinosum and stratum basale layers where 7-dehydrocholesterol is most abundant. No other organ or tissue in the body can synthesize vitamin D₃ from sunlight; the liver and kidneys later convert it (25-hydroxylation in the liver → 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in the kidneys), but the initial triggering and synthesis occur exclusively in the skin. Oral vitamin D (D₂ or D₃ from supplements/food) bypasses the skin step entirely.  So, in short: the skin is both the trigger and the site of vitamin D production in response to UVB exposure.1.1sFast

Does the retina have anything to do with Vitamin D production?
No, the retina has no role in vitamin D production.
 
Here’s the accurate breakdown:
Vitamin D₃ synthesis requires UVB photons (290–320 nm) to photolyze 7-dehydrocholesterol into previtamin D₃.
The retina is protected from UVB by multiple barriers:
The cornea absorbs almost all UVB below ~300 nm.
The lens (especially after age 25–30) filters out remaining UVB and most UVA.
By the time light reaches the retina, virtually zero UVB remains.

Experimental evidence confirms this:

Studies on animals and humans show that even intense ocular-only UV exposure (with the rest of the body shielded) does not raise serum 25(OH)D levels.
People who are completely blind or have had both eyes enucleated still produce normal amounts of vitamin D from skin exposure.
Conversely, covering all skin but exposing only the eyes to sunlight produces zero vitamin D.

There is one minor related finding (often misunderstood online):
The retina and suprachiasmatic nucleus (via the retinohypothalamic tract) detect visible blue light for circadian entrainment, which indirectly influences vitamin D metabolism by regulating time spent outdoors. But this is a behavioral/circadian effect, not direct vitamin D synthesis in the eye.

Bottom line: Vitamin D production is exclusively a skin function. The retina and eyes contribute nothing to it directly.

neutral.text:
Sorry - Kupfer ist ein relevantes Thema, aber Vit D ist sein Wissen mangelhaft - 9 Jahre Forschung und Anwendung widersprechen dem klar.

Die Aussage, dass synthetisches Vitamin D die Aufnahme von Vitamin A blockiert, ist nicht korrekt und basiert auf einem weit verbreiteten Missverständnis in manchen alternativen Gesundheitskreisen. Schauen wir uns die tatsächliche Wechselwirkung wissenschaftlich fundiert an:
Was wirklich passiert (evidenzbasierte Zusammenfassung):
	1	Vitamin D und Vitamin A sind Gegenspieler (Antagonisten) auf Rezeptorebene Beide Vitamine wirken über nukleäre Rezeptoren (VDR = Vitamin-D-Rezeptor, RAR/RXR = Retinsäure-/Retinoid-X-Rezeptoren). Hohe Dosen von einem können die Wirkung des anderen abschwächen – das ist seit Jahrzehnten bekannt (z. B. Studienergebnisse von Chris Masterjohn, Weston A. Price Foundation und ältere pharmakologische Studien). → Das ist aber kein Block der Aufnahme im Darm, sondern eine Konkurrenz um die gleichen Transportsysteme und Rezeptoren in den Zellen.
	2	Die Aufnahme im Darm wird nicht blockiert
	◦	Vitamin D (auch synthetisches Cholecalciferol oder Calcitriol) und Vitamin A (Retinol, Retinylpalmitat) werden über unterschiedliche Mechanismen aufgenommen.
	◦	Vitamin A wird größtenteils als Retinylester über Mizellen und CRBP II transportiert.
	◦	Vitamin D wird ebenfalls über Mizellen, aber dann über NPC1L1 und andere Transporter. → Es gibt keine relevante Konkurrenz auf Absorptionsebene im Darm bei normalen oder auch hohen physiologischen Dosen.
	3	Wo das eigentliche Problem liegt Bei sehr hohen Dosen (z. B. > 50.000–100.000 IE Vitamin D pro Tag über längere Zeit) ohne ausreichend Vitamin A und K2 kann es zu einer relativen Vitamin-A- und K2-Verarmung kommen – nicht durch Blockade der Aufnahme, sondern durch:
	◦	Stark erhöhten Bedarf an Vitamin A und K2 für die durch Vitamin D induzierten Proteine (z. B. Osteocalcin, MGP)
	◦	Verdrängung von Retinsäure an RXR-Rezeptoren durch aktivierte Vitamin-D-Formen
	4	Das kann zu Symptomen führen, die fälschlicherweise als „Vitamin-D-Vergiftung“ interpretiert werden, aber tatsächlich oft ein relativer Vitamin-A- und K2-Mangel sind.
Praktische Konsequenzen (2025-Stand der Forschung):
Situation
Risiko einer negativen Wechselwirkung?
Empfehlung
Normale Dosierung (2.000–10.000 IE D3) + normale Ernährung mit Vitamin A
Nein
Unbedenklich
Hohe D3-Dosen (> 20.000–50.000 IE/Tag) ohne extra A und K2
Ja (relativer A-/K2-Mangel möglich)
Vitamin A (ca. 5.000–10.000 IE/Tag) + K2 (MK-4 oder MK-7) ergänzen
Lebertran (natürliche Kombination A + D)
Sehr gering
Ideale natürliche Quelle
Synthetisches Vitamin D vs. natürliches
Kein Unterschied bez. A-Aufnahme
Synthetisches D3 ist genauso wirksam und sicher wie natürliches
Fazit:
Synthetisches Vitamin D blockiert NICHT die Aufnahme von Vitamin A im Darm. Die oft kolportierte „Blockade“ ist ein Mythos. Es gibt jedoch eine funktionelle Antagonismus bei sehr hohen Dosen, weshalb bei hochdosierter Vitamin-D-Therapie immer auf ausreichende Zufuhr von Vitamin A und besonders Vitamin K2 geachtet werden sollte.
Quellen (Auswahl):
	•	Cannell JJ et al. (Vitamin D Council)
	•	Masterjohn C. (2007–2024): From Seafood to Sunshine – umfangreiche Analysen
	•	Aburto et al. (2019): Vitamin A and D interactions
	•	Klinische Studien zu Hypervitaminose D und relativen Mangelzuständen
Falls du sehr hoch dosierst (> 20.000 IE D3/Tag), lass lieber Blutwerte (25-OH-D, Retinol, K2-Status wenn möglich) kontrollieren.

	1.	Bone Health
	•	Helps your body absorb calcium and phosphorus.
	•	Prevents bone loss, fractures, and conditions like osteoporosis.
	2.	Immune Support
	•	Regulates immune system function.

	4.	Muscle & Performance
	•	Supports muscle strength and coordination — handy if you’re active or playing golf.

	•	Heart health: some studies suggest benefits for blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.

This made me think of my little buddy Neo, I got him when I was around 12. My previous kitten had been run over in an accident a few years earlier and I blamed myself for not keeping a better eye on her and so I was scared to get another cat until I finally adopted Neo. He lived with us all the way through my adolescence and stayed at my parents when I moved out. 

He would “play soccer” with me as a kid. I would kick the ball in the backyard and he would chase the ball once it started moving, running alongside it getting ready to pounce and then at the last moment would abort his pounce - presumably realising that if he pounced on a soccer ball moving at speed he’d have got completely bowled over 😂 but he was always there, repeating this ritual - the ball triggering his ancient chase response! He was so fun to play with, almost like a dog - though I could never convince him to fetch, only chase lol.

He loved to lay down in front of the heater in the living room or on the heated bathroom floor and like me - had very little self control with food 😂 he kept eating till he would puke and we had to cover the other cat’s food so he wouldn’t eat it, silly boy. He would come and sleep on my bed purring away like a vibrating, living foot warmer at night. He also learned to call for his humans to let him in and out by running his paws down the glass rapidly making a funny, squeegee sort of noise on the glass door.

Even after I left home it always felt like he remembered and recognised me whenever I came home to visit. He passed away ~4 years ago. He was 19 I believe, my parents told me he was getting much more tired and less mobile but still holding on, curled up on the heated bathroom floor. We decided to let him pass naturally unless we had any reason to believe he was suffering. I came to see him for the last time, spoke to him, gently cuddled him and thanked him for everything and then he passed peacefully that night. It really felt like he was waiting to see me before he let go. 

We buried him in a raised bed directly under a beautiful new specimen tree. Neo’s tree has grown into a beautiful reminder of my old friend.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text:
I used to take Benadryl as over the counter medicine for hayfever. Haven't taken it for two plus years because I developed restless legs. 
I stopped taking atorvastatin 18 months ago, against my GPs advice. 
I took PPIs for short time (two weeks) to deal with health problem at the time, but no longer take it. 
Never taken benzodiazepines. 
I take perindopril 8mg for hypertension & CKD, and been taking it for over 10 years. 
I take tamsulosin after prostate cancer. 
I take tramadol 2 x 50mg up to three tines a day for Arthritic and lower back pain. I tapered off all doses until I stopped but actually found my pain WAS quite severe, so take two am and two pm. 
I have to take daily loperamide for chronic bowel issue following radiotherapy for prostate cancer. 
And finally, I take metformin for diabetes type 2. 
Your passion for polypharnacy is evident and I am very grateful for your channel and enthusiasm. 
Watching from 🇬🇧 🖐

positive.author: @sugeshnisanasey5930
positive.text:
OPTIONAL:

3Magnesium Glycinate
MANDATORY:
1.Fibre -Psyllium Husk

YOU'RE WELCOME😊

positive.author: @Marko964
positive.text:
Id go with

1. Omega 3  1-3g of Combined EPA and DHA per day. (i take 1.1g and might go up to 1.5 or 2).

Benefits: Systemic anti-inflammation, Brain/heart health, Supports skin barrier, reduces skin stress. 

2. Astaxanthin 12-18mg per day (I take 18mg)

Benefits: MAX Anti-inflammation, Cellular protection, Muscle recovery, Anti-aging protection, Eye Health, Increase in V02 max (Mixed Results), Reduced redness and a slight "Asta Glow" not a red orange tint. 
A study has shown it increases the life span of mice by 12%. Not done on humans yet but promising result.

3. Vitamin C 100-250 mg daily (i take 1000 every 4 days. Not as optimal but still good since it has a really long half life).

Benefits: Immune function, Powerful antioxidant, Essential for Collagen synthesis (skin firmness, joint health).

4. Magnesium L-Threonate or Glycinate 300-400 per day. (Usually it says not more then 350 but its meant for lesser versions like Magnesium Oxide. If u still wanna go safe then go with 200mg).

Magnesium L-Threonate
Brain/Cognitive Function

Magnesium Glycinate
Anxiety Relief, Muscle Relaxation, Sleep Aid

5. Vitamin D with K2 2000-10000 UI (i take 5000 UI) 100-300mcg (I take 200mcg).

Benefits: Strong Immunity, Hormonal support, Calcium absorption, Indirectly supports healthy cell turnover and mood. K2 regulating and directing calcium to bones and teeth while keeping it out of arteries, supporting strong bones, cardiovascular health, and preventing arterial calcification

6. Glycine 5-10g per day(Depending on ur goals even higher up to 90g.(I use 10g)

Benefits: MAX Deep Sleep Quality, Aids detoxification, Supports muscle repair (HGH release), Primary building block for Collagen, Supports skin hydration. 

Collagen made up of 33% of glycine. Some say less and others more. 

7. Zink (Optional) 5-15mg per day

Benefits: Immune function, DNA and cellular repair, Critical for skin healing, acne control, and hair/nail health.

8. Collagen (Optional) Slightly superior then Glycine for Looks but lacks the Big Boost on Sleep. And good sleep is the most important aspect of Health. Also called Beauty Sleep.

U will have to get the benefits of it urself since im not using it😅

9. Ashwaganda (Optional) Do ur own research on the best dose for u. I do 250mg of KSM-66. Above 300 for high stress and below for moderate. If u have low levels don’t bother buying it. 

Benefits: Manages Cortisol, Calms nervous system, aids sleep onset, Reduces stress-related inflammation and breakouts.

And if i missed some benefits feel free to add them.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text: To summarize: do FUNCTIONAL FITNESS.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @deanpaulson6714
positive.text:
Correctly applied exercise is really a phenomenon. I have a  50 years plus of sports performance however in my 50s a career in rugby and freestyle wrestling along with aggressive workouts wrecked my joints to the point that I literally gave up ! My health physical and mentally declined to a point that I stayed in bed and took pain meds barely able to move ( I awaiting a double hip and shoulder replacement) I couldn't even walk was literally suicidal , I was so attached to my past athletic level and fitness I thought it was all downhill.
 6 mths ago I decided to try and do something. I took a deep dive into studying isometrics it was literally all I could do in bed . Forward 6 mths I began learning and studying more and more patiently and carefully I began to devise mini 20 min workouts using long hold Isometrics (using a bed sheet ) 5 or 10 mins 2 or 3xday at first ( now up to 20 mins 4 or 5 x a day . I leaned how to combined in circuits to elevate my heart rate . I also took a deep dive into structural posture and  ROM . Forward 6 mths I'm now walking around moving my pain has decreased to a point that I am holding off on the surgeries. My muscle mass has returned , I got my diet and sleep more dialed in,  my mind is in a much better place. At 60 I'm not getting back on the wrestling mat but I will be able to play wrestle with my grandkids . The human body and mind can be a remarkable machine if you have the right mind set . Even if you are bed riden if you can contract muscle tissue you have hope .
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @vincenttacraebnam8379
positive.text:
I’ve noticed that those who suffer lifelong illnesses or conditions, many times outlive healthy. Injuries and not limiting or assessing risk of injury, sometimes costs years of life.
Injuries addition those that suffer for long and lifelong limitations, get better and informed and continuously monitor their health. My anecdotal group? My childhood friends - the “weak” outnumber in quality of life due to the “strong” being injured and sidelined. And then there’s the mental toughness or weakness…it is sometimes decisive.

*You can't fool me, you're not just discovering bone broth soup now, grandpa.* Bone broth isn't the magic fix for elderly Japanese folks struggling with hunched backs and wobbly legs. *Social media's full of pictures of older Japanese folks leaning on walkers, bent over looking at the ground unable to straighten up* and let's be real, all that bone broth didn't do much. *Clearly, there's more to mobility than just soup, no matter how many years they've been sipping it.*

Japan's got a super-aged society, where many seniors face mobility issues that make everyday life tough, like Locomotive Syndrome, which weakens bones, joints, and muscles, making it hard to stand or walk. This condition's a major reason seniors need nursing care. 

Spoiler Alert!!! Bone broth soup has been a staple in many cultures, especially among those who couldn't afford meat and relied on scraps. It's time to stop hyping up Japanese foods just because they sound exotic. 

Chefs worldwide have been making bone broth for ages, *so maybe take a seat and stop pretending you're the broth expert spreading misinformation.*

positive.author: @chazwyman
positive.text:
Milk is the only substance in nature—apart from honey—specifically designed to be eaten as food. As mammals, we produce milk that contains nearly all the nutrition required for energy, growth, and maintenance. That means we need a very strong reason to dismiss dairy entirely.

Milk’s purpose, however, is growth, and that can be a drawback for adults who have already finished growing. It is unusual in nature to find protein, fat, and carbohydrates together in one food, and milk’s ratios promote growth and can also be somewhat addictive.

Cream, butter, cheese, and yoghurt reduce this issue because their composition is altered through fermentation or separation. These foods remain highly nutritious and are among the best whole-food options available.

The closest rival to milk as a complete food is the egg, which contains everything required to create new life.

transcript.summary: The speaker discusses the limitations of VO2 max as a predictor of health span and argues that focusing on functional capacity is more important.

positive.author: @kwikstep-1
positive.text: I am 87 yrs old, male, retired peon not well educated. I never knew what V02 max is. I just do my exercise of choice & to reach 87 yrs of age .,My Own exercise puts emphasis on life enjoyment while exercising at the same time engaging in social interaction & mental stimulation. For Over 21 yrs. all I did and still doing it is by dancing to several Variety of dancing styles such as Ballroom, Latin, like Salsa Bachata, All the Swing dances, Hustle dance Etc. I dance 4 to 5 times a week,for at least 2 to 3 hrs. Dancing keep me keep me physically active & fit, MENTALLY Sharp, & most of all Enjoying life while exercising. Regardless of what my VO2 max is.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @ncournault
positive.text:
Nassim Nicholas Taleb made a great point on X about VO2Max recently. He said that the research shows that a LOW VO2Max is a good predictor of mortality and poor health but a HIGH VO2Max isn't a good predictor of lifespan and good health.
In other words, a low VO2Max will most certainly lead you to early death and morbidity but a high one doesn't necessarily add years to your life or extends you healthspan.
This resonates well with the advice  offered in this video. You absolutely can't afford a low VO2max, but chasing an elite level reading might be fool's gold. 
And, yes, doing 2 hours a day of Z1/Z2 cardio will leave you  unable to train all the other equally important components of healthspan like mobility, balance, strength, communal activities....
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @alexanderilinskiy9926
positive.text: It is genius and simple at the same time. A kind of an integrated approach to a humanbeeing as a system. We would like not only live longer but also function. We need funcional living. Very important to be fit and keep an eye on one`s function abilities using your simple tests not to overlook blind spots in any domain. Deep respect to you and your research!  It is a pity I cannot buy your books  because of sanctions. I wish you further success in all your projects. People need it.
positive.label: Positive

positive.author: @grahambowes756
positive.text: Thanks. And I find that a mix of exercise works well for me. As well as the hiking I’m a keen road cyclist. But totally agree that genetics play a big role here. As I approach 70, I’m lucky to have low RHR at 42bpm, reasonably high MHR at 177bpm. And reasonable VO2 Max around 46 trending up after an exercise break for surgery.  I feel like my long term consistency have helped preserve fast twitch muscle fibre and endurance. and I do feel the benefits in everyday life. I’d encourage anyone who is able, to exercise more. Don’t think you’ve left it too late. Improvement is there to be realised. All the best from the UK.
positive.label: Positive

Summarising the 25 Habits -

1. Don't chase for happiness. 
2. Use chopsticks daily
3. Bowing. Straighten spine and correct the core.
4. Soak bath seriously at 40°C for 15mins.
5. Eat the whole fish.
6. Practice meditation. Stillness and mindfulness
7. Drink barley tea daily
8. Integrate workouts into the daily movement
9. Use squat toilet. Help clear bowels.
10. Sleep in total darkness.
11. Wash and scrab the hands clean seriously
12. Cool down with hand fans
13. Forest bathing. Walk slowly mindfully in forest.
14. Walking bare foot on purpose.
15. Sit on the floor
16. Use smaller utensils. Control the amount consumed
17. Eat seasonal food.
18. Eat with full dedication. No phone when dining.
19. Keep belly/core warm.
20. Adapt to cold weather. Best between 14-18°C to burn body brown fats.
21. Walk 7-9k steps. Brisk purposeful walking
22. Eat 1 fermented food every meal
23. Do not snack. 
24. Gargle salt water 1~2 times a day.
25. Prolonged Chewing. Chew 30-50times. Consume 80℅ full by eating slowly.

Protein needs:
 General Recommendations (Grams per kg of body weight)
Healthy, Active Seniors: 1.0 - 1.2 g/kg/day.
Ill or Injured Seniors: 1.2 - 1.5 g/kg/day.
Active Seniors (Exercise): Can aim for 1.4 - 2 g/kg/day. 
How to Calculate Your Needs
Convert your weight: Divide your weight in pounds by 2.2 to get your weight in kilograms (kg).
Multiply by your target: Multiply your weight in kg by your recommended protein factor (e.g., 1.2) to find your daily grams. 
Example: A 75 kg (165 lb.) man aiming for 1.2 g/kg/day needs about 90 grams of protein daily (75 kg * 1.2 g/kg).

Protein needs:
 General Recommendations (Grams per kg of body weight)
Healthy, Active Seniors: 1.0 - 1.2 g/kg/day.
Ill or Injured Seniors: 1.2 - 1.5 g/kg/day.
Active Seniors (Exercise): Can aim for 1.4 - 2 g/kg/day. 
How to Calculate Your Needs
Convert your weight: Divide your weight in pounds by 2.2 to get your weight in kilograms (kg).
Multiply by your target: Multiply your weight in kg by your recommended protein factor (e.g., 1.2) to find your daily grams. 
Example: A 75 kg (165 lb.) man aiming for 1.2 g/kg/day needs about 90 grams of protein daily (75 kg * 1.2 g/kg).

neutral.author: @RealBibleAnswered
neutral.text:
This diet is a textbook example of a "microbiome-centric" approach. From a clinical nutrition standpoint, it hits the gold standard for gut health by prioritizing the Three Ps (Probiotics, Prebiotics, and Polyphenols) and aiming for that magic number of 30+ grams of fiber daily.

However, "good for you" is relative. Here is the brutally honest breakdown of why this works and where it might actually cause you problems.

The Good: Why Your Microbiome Would Love This
Diversity is King: The "Rainforest" analogy for the gut is accurate. By using chickpeas, multiple bean varieties, nuts, seeds, and whole grains, she is feeding different strains of bacteria. A diverse gut is a resilient gut.

Polyphenol Power: The inclusion of matcha and 85% dark chocolate is smart. Polyphenols aren't just antioxidants; they act as prebiotics that specifically encourage the growth of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus.

Circadian Rhythm Support: The 12-hour "gut rest" (fasting window) is perhaps the most underrated part of this plan. It allows for the Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) to sweep through the GI tract, clearing out waste and preventing bacterial overgrowth (SIBO).

The Bad: Why Your Physical Gut Might Hate This
The "Fiber Bomb" Effect: If you aren't currently eating a high-fiber diet, switching to this overnight would be a disaster. You are looking at significant bloating, gas, and potential cramping. The Myota supplement on top of chickpeas, beans, and whole grains is a massive amount of substrate for fermentation.

Antinutrients: Chickpeas and beans are high in lectins and phytates. For some, these can irritate the gut lining rather than soothe it. If you have a sensitive system, "fully loaded" legumes at every meal might be inflammatory.

Bioavailability: While she stresses "plant-forward," this diet is low in easily absorbable fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, K2) and B12, which are usually found in animal fats. The avocado helps, but it’s a lean profile.

The Verdict
Is it good for your gut? Generally, yes—it promotes a thriving microbial ecosystem.
Is it good for you? Only if your digestion is already "trained" for high volume.

Here is the "brutally honest" breakdown of the vitamins, minerals, and bone health implications of this specific meal plan.

1. The Mineral Absorption "Wall" (Phytates & Oxalates)
The biggest threat to bone health in this diet isn't a lack of minerals, but the inability to absorb them.

The Problem: Chickpeas (lunch/snack), various beans (dinner), and whole grains (breakfast/lunch) are loaded with phytates. Matcha and dark chocolate are high in oxalates.

The Bone Impact: These "anti-nutrients" bind to calcium, magnesium, and zinc in the digestive tract, preventing them from being absorbed into your bloodstream. If you eat a "fully loaded" chickpea sandwich and wash it down with matcha, you might only absorb a fraction of the calcium present in those foods.

The Fix: You must soak or sprout your legumes and grains. If you’re just opening a can of chickpeas and tossing them in a bowl, you are likely hitting a "mineral wall."

2. The Missing "Bone-Building" Duo: Vitamin D and K2
Bone health is a construction project: Calcium is the brick, but Vitamin D is the delivery truck and Vitamin K2 is the foreman who tells the calcium where to go.

The Gap: This diet is virtually devoid of Vitamin K2. While K1 is found in plants (like the spinach or jalapeño in the chili), K2—which prevents calcium from depositing in your arteries and shunts it into your bones—is primarily found in animal fats, egg yolks, and fermented foods like natto.

The Vitamin D Trap: Unless your yogurt or cereal is heavily fortified, there is very little Vitamin D here. Without it, your body cannot absorb the calcium from the yogurt or beans efficiently.

3. The Protein-Bone Paradox
Your bones are actually about 50% protein by volume.

The Observation: This diet relies heavily on plant-based proteins (chickpeas, beans). While these are great for the microbiome, they are less "dense" in essential amino acids than animal proteins.

The Risk: If your total protein intake is too low (common in "plant-forward" diets if not carefully tracked), your body may prioritize other functions over bone remodeling.

4. The "Gut-Bone Axis" (The Secret Advantage)
There is a silver lining. Dr. Prpa’s approach relies on Short-Chain Fatty Acids (SCFAs) like butyrate, which are produced when your gut bacteria ferment all that fiber.

The Benefit: Research shows that SCFAs can actually signal osteoblasts (bone-building cells) to increase activity and reduce systemic inflammation that breaks down bone.

The Strategy: By feeding the microbiome with the "diversity bowl," you are creating a chemical environment that supports bone density from the inside out—provided you are actually getting the raw materials (Calcium/D3/K2) from elsewhere.
The "Brutal" Summary
If you follow this diet exactly as written without supplementation or specific food prep (soaking/sprouting), you are at risk for sub-optimal bone density over time. The "gut health" wins, but the "skeletal health" may lose due to poor absorption.


Breakfast: A yogurt bowl featuring live yogurt (probiotics), matcha granola (polyphenols from green tea), microwaved frozen berries (fiber), and a scoop of Myota fiber blend (prebiotics and extra fiber)—all emphasizing a plant-forward approach with the three Ps: plants/prebiotics, probiotics, and polyphenols.

Lunch: A fully loaded chickpea bowl on whole grain bread (fiber-rich legumes and grains), described as a "gut health sonnie" with chickpeas as the star for their fiber content to feed gut bacteria.

Snack: Peppermint tea (for gut relaxation) and prebiotic rocky road made with chickpeas, nuts, seeds (fiber), and 85% dark chocolate (polyphenols).

Dinner: Chili bean diversity bowl with various fibrous beans in chili, whole grain rice (balanced carbs and fiber), avocado (healthy fats), and creamy jalapeño nacho chips on the side for joy—highlighting plant diversity like a "rainforest" for the microbiome.

Throughout the day, she stresses hydration to pair with high-fiber meals, slow chewing, and no eating close to bedtime for a 12-hour gut rest.

The Myota supplement on top of chickpeas, beans, and whole grains is a massive amount of substrate for fermentation.

Antinutrients: Chickpeas and beans are high in lectins and phytates. For some, these can irritate the gut lining rather than soothe it. If you have a sensitive system, "fully loaded" legumes at every meal might be inflammatory.

Bioavailability: While she stresses "plant-forward," this diet is low in easily absorbable fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, K2) and B12, which are usually found in animal fats. The avocado helps, but it’s a lean profile.

The Verdict
Is it good for your gut? Generally, yes—it promotes a thriving microbial ecosystem.
Is it good for you? Only if your digestion is already "trained" for high volume.

Here is the "brutally honest" breakdown of the vitamins, minerals, and bone health implications of this specific meal plan.

1. The Mineral Absorption "Wall" (Phytates & Oxalates)
The biggest threat to bone health in this diet isn't a lack of minerals, but the inability to absorb them.

The Problem: Chickpeas (lunch/snack), various beans (dinner), and whole grains (breakfast/lunch) are loaded with phytates. Matcha and dark chocolate are high in oxalates.

The Bone Impact: These "anti-nutrients" bind to calcium, magnesium, and zinc in the digestive tract, preventing them from being absorbed into your bloodstream. If you eat a "fully loaded" chickpea sandwich and wash it down with matcha, you might only absorb a fraction of the calcium present in those foods.

The Fix: You must soak or sprout your legumes and grains. If you’re just opening a can of chickpeas and tossing them in a bowl, you are likely hitting a "mineral wall."

2. The Missing "Bone-Building" Duo: Vitamin D and K2
Bone health is a construction project: Calcium is the brick, but Vitamin D is the delivery truck and Vitamin K2 is the foreman who tells the calcium where to go.

The Gap: This diet is virtually devoid of Vitamin K2. While K1 is found in plants (like the spinach or jalapeño in the chili), K2—which prevents calcium from depositing in your arteries and shunts it into your bones—is primarily found in animal fats, egg yolks, and fermented foods like natto.

The Vitamin D Trap: Unless your yogurt or cereal is heavily fortified, there is very little Vitamin D here. Without it, your body cannot absorb the calcium from the yogurt or beans efficiently.

3. The Protein-Bone Paradox
Your bones are actually about 50% protein by volume.

The Observation: This diet relies heavily on plant-based proteins (chickpeas, beans). While these are great for the microbiome, they are less "dense" in essential amino acids than animal proteins.

The Risk: If your total protein intake is too low (common in "plant-forward" diets if not carefully tracked), your body may prioritize other functions over bone remodeling.

4. The "Gut-Bone Axis" (The Secret Advantage)
There is a silver lining. Dr. Prpa’s approach relies on Short-Chain Fatty Acids (SCFAs) like butyrate, which are produced when your gut bacteria ferment all that fiber.

The Benefit: Research shows that SCFAs can actually signal osteoblasts (bone-building cells) to increase activity and reduce systemic inflammation that breaks down bone.

The Strategy: By feeding the microbiome with the "diversity bowl," you are creating a chemical environment that supports bone density from the inside out—provided you are actually getting the raw materials (Calcium/D3/K2) from elsewhere.
The "Brutal" Summary
If you follow this diet exactly as written without supplementation or specific food prep (soaking/sprouting), you are at risk for sub-optimal bone density over time. The "gut health" wins, but the "skeletal health" may lose due to poor absorption.


Breakfast: A yogurt bowl featuring live yogurt (probiotics), matcha granola (polyphenols from green tea), microwaved frozen berries (fiber), and a scoop of Myota fiber blend (prebiotics and extra fiber)—all emphasizing a plant-forward approach with the three Ps: plants/prebiotics, probiotics, and polyphenols.

Lunch: A fully loaded chickpea bowl on whole grain bread (fiber-rich legumes and grains), described as a "gut health sonnie" with chickpeas as the star for their fiber content to feed gut bacteria.

Snack: Peppermint tea (for gut relaxation) and prebiotic rocky road made with chickpeas, nuts, seeds (fiber), and 85% dark chocolate (polyphenols).

Dinner: Chili bean diversity bowl with various fibrous beans in chili, whole grain rice (balanced carbs and fiber), avocado (healthy fats), and creamy jalapeño nacho chips on the side for joy—highlighting plant diversity like a "rainforest" for the microbiome.

Throughout the day, she stresses hydration to pair with high-fiber meals, slow chewing, and no eating close to bedtime for a 12-hour gut rest.

Benefits: Prevents telomeres from shortening (slowing cellular aging) and supports natural cellular repair.

Dr. Li's Tip: Add a squeeze of lemon to help your body absorb the antioxidants better. Avoid adding milk, as it can block the absorption of certain nutrients.

positive.author: @CardrossWestwood
positive.text: One of my favourite keto-friendly breakfasts is egg-drop soup. Just make up a cup of quality chicken stock. Bring it to a boil in a small pan on the stove top. Drop in a small handful of chopped spring onions (I keep a bag of them in my freezer; you can cook from frozen). Add a pinch of chilli pepper flakes if you like spice. Then whisk up 1 egg and dribble it all into the boiling stock. Don't stir it! Just drop it in and the boiling water will cook it in an instant. I always have eggs and chicken stock and frozen spring onions at hand, so this is quick and easy to make.

negative.text:
Keuth, S., & Bisping, B. (1994). Vitamin B12 production by Citrobacter freundii during tempeh fermentation. Applied and Environmental Microbiology.

Any form of soya that isn't sprouted and fermented is an anti-nutrient vehicle. Anti-elastase or anti-trypsin is reduced by sprouting and further by fermentation.

We require Trypsin and the other proteases to resolve proteins to amino acids. When the natural SERPINs (serine protease inhibitors) are not eliminated or greatly reduced, we stress our pancreas to resynthesize the debilitated proteases. Eventually this can induce an enlarged pancreas and enlargement can result in inflammation. Inflammation can result in constriction of blood supply and cell death, before one knows it pancreatitis results.  The pancreas is a vital organ, so when induced to regenerate lacking the surveillance enzymes that control regeneration mediating cells, trophoblasts, the process can result in patent cancers.

positive.text:
After carefully watching this full video from start to finish, I’ve put together a simple numbered summary with timestamps so it’s easier for everyone to follow and apply:

1. Vitamin C (Collagen support + circulation + reduce leg fatigue) — 02:17
2. Vitamin D3 + K2 + Magnesium (Muscle power, balance & fall prevention system) — 06:42
3. Vitamin B12 – Methylcobalamin (Nerve repair + coordination + leg responsiveness) — 11:32

I’ve simplified this breakdown so older adults can follow the key points more clearly without feeling overwhelmed while watching. May these small insights help you move with more confidence, stay independent longer, and continue living a healthy, steady, and peaceful life each day.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text:
I’m 65. Burning, walking on rocks, tingling and electrical shock feelings in hands and feet. My doctor gave me Gabapentin then after a couple of years, my nerves were flaring so she put me on Lyrica. It stopped the flaring, but not the other symptoms. It even hurts to sit in a chair, because it’s all the nerves in my legs. My hands/fingers tingle all day. 

I have Multiple Myeloma and the chemotherapy has ruined my nerves. I pray that what you’re saying will help me. Love you.💜

I can’t keep up with you  to write it down let alone know how to spell the kind, to look for has … in it. Can’t you show this information on the screen and leave it up there for a good length of time for us older people to be able to write it down?  Or put a list in the description, this way we could enjoy listening to what you’re saying,  knowing that we will be able to find all the information in the description?  

Otherwise, I honestly am already tired of rewinding the video so many times, and I can’t really take in all the wonderful information you’re trying to share with us. I would assume many other people too, have this issue.
positive.label: Positive

positive.text:
One more thing I want to point out. With some cancers, there are no symptoms until it's too late. I was diagnosed with stage 3, grade 3 HER2+ breast cancer. I had no symptoms at all. I felt great, had loads of energy, and had no idea anything was wrong. I had had a mammogram 5 months earlier, and nothing showed up then, but HER2 is very aggressive and quick. If I had waited until my next mammogram, I probably wouldn't be here now.
My little dog is the one who found my cancer. He suddenly got very needy and wanted me to hold him all the time. When I picked him up, he would burrow into my chest and sometimes try to dig or press up against me. This went on for several weeks until one time he pushed so hard against me, I felt the lump. I credit this little 6-pound dog for saving my life.

negative.text: There's no doubt carbs increase performance, but only up to a point. You mentioned that training is "hard enough" without reducing carbs, but most training for endurance athletes is supposed to be easy! If you are feeling such a difference from taking in 15g of carbs from apple sauce for a 30 minute jog, that just says that you're not metabolically flexible, or you have severely depleted your glycogen the previous day, and not eaten anything since!

positive.text:
以下是針對 **STEPHEN PHINNEY | KETONES …cut inflammation; preferred by HEART; support liver | DoctorsToTrust** 的重點摘要與補充評論：

---

## 🔎 內容摘要

Stephen Phinney 博士主要說明「酮體（Ketones）」對身體的重要作用，尤其在低醣或生酮飲食狀態下的影響：

### 1⃣ 酮體能降低發炎（Cut Inflammation）

* 酮體（特別是 β-hydroxybutyrate）不只是能量來源，也是一種訊號分子。
* 它可以抑制發炎反應，例如降低某些發炎相關的發炎小體（inflammasome）活性。
* 因此對慢性發炎疾病可能有幫助。

### 2⃣ 心臟偏好酮體作為燃料（Preferred by the Heart）

* 心臟其實很「喜歡」使用酮體。
* 在某些情況下（例如心臟衰竭），心臟使用酮體的效率比葡萄糖更好。
* 酮體提供穩定、乾淨的能量來源。

### 💕💕3⃣ 支持肝臟功能（Support Liver）

* 酮體是由肝臟製造。
* 當身體進入生酮狀態時，肝臟會有效地轉換脂肪為酮體。
* 有研究指出，適當的生酮飲食可能有助於改善脂肪肝。

---

## 💬 補充評論

### ✔ 優點

* 近年研究確實支持酮體具有抗發炎與代謝調節功能。
* 心臟在代謝彈性（metabolic flexibility）方面，確實可以有效利用酮體。
* 生酮飲食對某些代謝症候群患者可能有幫助。

### ⚠💕💕 需要注意的地方

* 並非每個人都適合長期生酮飲食。
* 有肝臟或腎臟疾病者應諮詢醫師。
* 生酮飲食若執行不當（例如高加工肉類、油脂品質不佳）可能反而增加風險。
* 目前多數研究仍在持續進行中，並非所有效果都已完全確立。

---

## 🧠 簡單總結

酮體不只是「備用燃料」，它還可能：

* 幫助降低發炎
* 為心臟提供有效能量
* 在某些情況下支持肝臟健康

但是否適合自己，仍需根據個人體質與健康狀況來評估。

---

如果您希望，我也可以幫您整理成：

* 📌 條列式筆記版
* 📊 生酮飲食優缺點比較表
* 🫀❤❤ 心臟與酮體的科學機制說明
* 🧾 或是更生活化、白話版本

請告訴我您想要哪一種 😊

Propaganda always sucks, but medical propaganda kills.
